name: Exodus
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Dead Sea Scrolls of Exodus as reported in general terms. Every Septuagint reading cited in the footnotes was checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation of the Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus, with Codex Alexandrinus where it differs). Readings of the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Dead Sea Scrolls, and other ancient versions are stated in general terms until they can be checked against the critical editions. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; where the Hebrew numbering differs (7:26 to 8:28 and 21:37 to 22:30 in Hebrew), a footnote says so. Measurements are given in modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes.

verses.text: These are the names{a} of the sons of Israel who came into Egypt with Jacob; each man came with his household:
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
All the persons descended from Jacob{b} numbered seventy.{c} Joseph was already in Egypt.
Then Joseph died, and all his brothers, and all that generation.
The Israelites were fruitful and swarmed;{d} they became numerous and grew exceedingly mighty, and the land was full of them.
Then a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph.
He said to his people, “See, the people of the Israelites are too many and too mighty for us.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will multiply, and if war breaks out, they will join our enemies, fight against us, and go up out of the land.”
So they set taskmasters over them to oppress them with forced labor. They built supply cities for Pharaoh:{e} Pithom and Rameses.{f}
Yet the harder they were oppressed, the more they increased and spread abroad, and the Egyptians grew to dread the Israelites.
The Egyptians made the Israelites work ruthlessly.
They embittered their lives with harsh service, with mortar and bricks and all manner of labor in the fields; in every task in which they worked them, they were ruthless.
Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one named Shiphrah and the other named Puah.{g}
He said, “When you act as midwife to the Hebrew women and look upon the birthstool,{h} if it is a boy, you shall put him to death, but if it is a girl, she shall live.”
The midwives, however, feared God. They did not do what the king of Egypt had commanded them, and they kept the boys alive.
So the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and said to them, “Why have you done this and let the boys live?”
The midwives answered Pharaoh, “Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women; they are vigorous{i} and have given birth before the midwife arrives.”
So God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very strong.
Because the midwives feared God, he gave them households of their own.{j}
Pharaoh then gave this command to all his people: “Every boy who is born{k} you shall cast into the Nile, but every girl you shall keep alive.”

notes.text: Hebrew we’elleh shemot, “and these are the names.” The opening words, Shemot (“Names”), are the Hebrew title of the book. The English title Exodus comes from the Greek Exodos, “departure.”
Hebrew “who came out of Jacob’s thigh,” a Hebrew way of saying his direct descendants.

The Septuagint and a Dead Sea Scroll of Exodus read “seventy-five,” the number Stephen gives in Acts 7:14. Genesis 46:27 gives seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-five in the Septuagint, which counts additional descendants of Joseph.
Or “teemed.” The verbs echo the creation blessing of Genesis 1:28 and 9:1.
Pharaoh is a title meaning “great house,” that is, the royal palace. Exodus never gives the personal name of the king.
The Septuagint adds “and On, which is Heliopolis.”

Shiphrah probably means “beautiful” and Puah perhaps “splendid” or “girl”; both meanings are uncertain. Both names are attested among Semitic names of the period. The Hebrew can also be read “the midwives of the Hebrews,” leaving open whether they were themselves Hebrews or Egyptians.
Hebrew “on the two stones,” probably the stones a woman crouched on to give birth.
Or “lively.” The Hebrew word occurs only here; it is related to the word for “living,” or perhaps to the word for “animal,” in the sense “they give birth easily, like animals.”
Literally “he made houses for them,” that is, he gave them families.
The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Targums add “to the Hebrews.”

verses.text: Now a man from the house of Levi went and married a daughter of Levi.{a}
The woman conceived and bore a son. When she saw that he was a fine{b} child, she hid him three months.
When she was no longer able to hide him, she got a papyrus basket{c} for him and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She placed the child in it and laid it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile.
His sister stationed herself at a distance to find out what would happen to him.
Then Pharaoh’s daughter came down to bathe at the Nile, while her young women walked along beside the Nile. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant girl to get it.
When she opened it, she saw the child, and there was the boy, crying. She had pity on him and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Shall I go and call a nursing woman from the Hebrews to nurse the child for you?”
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Go.” So the young woman went and called the child’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages.” So the woman took the child and nursed him.
The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became a son to her. She called his name Moses,{d} saying, “For I drew him out of the water.”
In those days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his people{e} and looked at their forced labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people.
He looked this way and that, and when he saw no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
He went out the next day, and there were two Hebrew men fighting. He said to the one in the wrong, “Why are you striking your fellow Hebrew?”
But he said, “Who appointed you as prince and judge over us? Do you intend to slay me, as you slew the Egyptian?” Moses was frightened and thought, “Surely the matter has become known.”
When Pharaoh heard about this matter, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian,{f} and he sat down by a well.
Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock.
Then the shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up, came to their rescue, and watered their flock.
When they came to their father Reuel,{g} he said, “Why have you come back so soon today?”
They said, “An Egyptian rescued us from the hand of the shepherds. He even drew water for us and watered the flock.”
He said to his daughters, “Where is he, then? Why did you abandon the man? Call him in to eat bread.”
Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah{h} as wife.
She bore a son, and he named him Gershom,{i} for he said, “I have become a foreigner in a foreign land.”{j}
In those many days{k} the king of Egypt died. The Israelites sighed because of their slavery and cried out; their plea for help from their bondage rose up to God.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
God saw the Israelites, and God knew.{l}

notes.text: The parents are named in 6:20 as Amram and Jochebed.
Hebrew tov, “good,” the word used in Genesis 1 when God saw that what he made was good.
Hebrew tevah, the word used for Noah’s ark (Genesis 6–9) and nowhere else in the Bible.

The Hebrew name Mosheh sounds like mashah, “to draw out”; in form it means “one who draws out.” It also resembles the Egyptian word mose, “is born” or “son,” found in names such as Thutmose and Ahmose.
Hebrew “his brothers,” here and in the rest of the verse (“one of his brothers”).
Midian was a people of northwest Arabia and the Sinai region, descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:2).
Reuel means “friend of God.” He is also called Jethro (3:1; 18:1) and, in Numbers 10:29, Moses’ father-in-law is called “Hobab son of Reuel.”
Zipporah means “bird.”
Gershom sounds like ger sham, “a foreigner there.”

Some ancient witnesses, including some Septuagint manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate, add: “She conceived again and bore a son, and he named him Eliezer, saying, ‘The God of my father is my help and has rescued me from the hand of Pharaoh.’” Compare 18:4.
Hebrew “in those many days.”
Literally “and God knew,” without an object. The Septuagint reads “and he made himself known to them.” The sense is that God took notice of their condition.

verses.text: Moses was tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro,{a} the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb,{b} the mountain of God.
The angel of Yahweh{c} appeared to him in a flame of fire from the middle of a bush.{d} He looked, and there was the bush, burning with fire, yet the bush was not consumed.
Moses said, “I must turn aside and see this great sight, why the bush does not burn up.”
Yahweh saw that he turned aside to see, and God called to him out of the midst of the bush: “Moses, Moses!” And he answered, “Here I am.”
Then he said, “Come no closer. Remove your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.”
He also said, “I am the God of your father,{e} the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
Then Yahweh said, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt. I have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings.

So I have come down to deliver them from the power of the Egyptians and to bring them up from that land into a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey,{f} to the place of the Canaanites and the Hittites and the Amorites and the Perizzites and the Hivites and the Jebusites.{g}
Behold, the outcry of the Israelites has reached me, and I myself have seen the oppression with which the Egyptians are oppressing them.
So now go. I am sending you to Pharaoh, so that you may bring my people, the Israelites, out of Egypt.”
But Moses said to God, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?”
He said, “I will be with you.{h} And this will be the sign for you that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.”
Then Moses said to God, “Suppose I come to the Israelites and say to them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ What shall I tell them?”
God said to Moses, “I am who I am.”{i} And he said, “This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I am{j} has sent me to you.’”

God also said to Moses, “This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘Yahweh,{k} the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered from generation to generation.{l}

“Go and assemble the elders of Israel and say to them, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—has appeared to me and said, “I have surely taken note of you{m} and of what is being done to you in Egypt.

I have promised to bring you up from the affliction of Egypt into the land of the Canaanites and the Hittites and the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites—a land that flows with milk and honey.”’

They will heed your voice. Then you and the elders of Israel shall go in to the king of Egypt and say to him, ‘Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, has encountered us; now, we ask, let us go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to Yahweh our God.’
But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless he is forced by a mighty hand.{n}
So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders that I will do among them. After that he will let you go.
And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that when you go, you will not go empty-handed.

Each woman shall ask her neighbor, and any woman who lodges in her house, for silver articles and gold articles and for garments; you shall put these on your sons and daughters, and so you shall strip the Egyptians.”

notes.text: Jethro probably means “abundance” or “excellence.” He is called Reuel in 2:18.
Horeb, meaning “dry” or “desolate,” is another name for Mount Sinai.

Yahweh is the personal name of God, written in Hebrew with the four letters YHWH. This is its first appearance in Exodus; on its meaning, see the note at 3:15. Here “the angel of Yahweh” is soon identified with Yahweh himself (verse 4).
Hebrew seneh, a thorny bush, probably a kind of bramble or acacia. The word sounds like Sinai.
The Samaritan Pentateuch and some Septuagint manuscripts read “fathers,” as in verses 13 and 15.
A traditional description of a fertile land good for grazing (milk from goats and sheep) and for bees or fruit (honey can also mean syrup made from dates or figs).
The list of the peoples of Canaan varies in length and order; the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch often add the Girgashites to make seven peoples, as in Deuteronomy 7:1.
Hebrew ki ehyeh immak, “for I will be with you.” The verb ehyeh (“I will be”) prepares for the name God gives in verse 14.

Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh. The verb hayah, “to be,” in this form can mean “I am,” “I will be,” or “I become,” so the phrase can also be translated “I will be who I will be” or “I am the one who is.” The Septuagint translates “I am the one who exists” (ego eimi ho on). The name expresses God’s self-existence, his faithful presence with his people (verse 12), and his freedom to make himself known as he chooses.
Hebrew ehyeh, “I am” or “I will be,” the first word of verse 14 used as a name. The Septuagint reads “The one who is has sent me.”

Hebrew YHWH, God’s personal name, which occurs about 6,800 times in the Hebrew Bible. Here God explains it by the verb in verse 14: ehyeh (“I am”) is the name in God’s own mouth, and YHWH (“he is” or “he will be”) is the same name spoken by others about him. Ancient Hebrew was written without vowels, and from the centuries before Christ onward, Jews out of reverence stopped pronouncing the name and read Adonai, “Lord,” in its place. The Septuagint translated it kyrios, “Lord,” and most English Bibles print “the LORD.” The pronunciation Yahweh is supported by early Christian writers who give it in Greek as Iaoue and Iabe, and by the short form Yah (15:2) and names such as Elijah and Isaiah. The form “Jehovah” arose later by combining the consonants YHWH with the vowels of Adonai. This translation writes the name as Yahweh throughout.
Literally “and this is my remembrance from generation to generation.”
Or “I have surely visited you,” that is, come to your aid. Joseph used the same words in Genesis 50:24–25.
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “except by a mighty hand,” and some interpreters read the Hebrew “not even by a mighty hand,” meaning that only the plagues will break his resistance.

verses.text: Moses answered, “But what if they will not believe me or listen to my voice, and say, ‘Yahweh did not appear to you’?”
Yahweh said to him, “What is that in your hand?” He said, “A staff.”
He said, “Throw it on the ground.” So he threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and Moses ran from it.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand and seize it by the tail.” He stretched out his hand and took hold of it, and it turned into a staff in his palm.
“This is so that they may believe that Yahweh, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”
Yahweh also said to him, “Put your hand inside your cloak.” So he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, there was his hand, diseased,{a} white as snow.
He said, “Return your hand to your bosom.” So he returned his hand to his bosom, and when he brought it out of his bosom, it was restored like the rest of his flesh.
“If they will not believe you or listen to the voice of the first sign, they may believe the voice of the second sign.

And if they will not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground. The water you take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground.”

But Moses said to Yahweh, “Please, Lord,{b} I have never been eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant; for I am slow in speaking and slow in tongue.”
Yahweh said to him, “Who put a mouth on humankind?{c} Or who makes someone mute or deaf, sighted or blind? Is it not I, Yahweh?
So now go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you are to say.”
But he said, “Please, Lord, send someone else, anyone you will send.”{d}

Yahweh’s anger flared against Moses. He said, “Is not Aaron{e} the Levite your brother? I know that he speaks well. Now see, he is on his way out to meet you, and when he sees you he will rejoice in his heart.
You will speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will teach you both what you are to do.
He will speak for you to the people. He will be a mouth for you, and you will be like God to him.{f}
And take this staff in your hand, with which you will do the signs.”

Moses departed and returned to Jether,{g} his father-in-law, and said to him, “Let me go, I pray, and return to my kinsmen who are in Egypt, and see whether they are still living.” Jethro said to Moses, “Go in peace.”
Yahweh said to Moses in Midian, “Go, return to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead.”
Moses took his wife and his sons, set them upon a donkey, and returned to the land of Egypt; and the staff of God was in his hand.
Yahweh said to Moses, “As you go back to Egypt, take care to do before Pharaoh all the wonders that I have placed in your hand. But I will harden{h} his heart, so that he will not release the people.
Then you are to say to Pharaoh, ‘This is what Yahweh says: Israel is my son, my firstborn.
I said to you, “Let my son go, so that he may serve me.” But you refused to let him go. So now I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”
On the way, at a lodging place, Yahweh met him{i} and sought to put him to death.
Then Zipporah took a flint knife and cut her son’s foreskin, and she touched it to his feet{j} and said, “You are indeed a bridegroom of blood to me!”
So he let him go. She had said “bridegroom of blood” on account of the circumcision.{k}
Yahweh said to Aaron, “Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.” So he went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all the words of Yahweh with which he had sent him, and all the signs he had commanded him to do.
Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the Israelites.
Aaron told them all the words that Yahweh had spoken to Moses, and he did the signs before the eyes of the people.
The people believed; and when they heard that Yahweh had visited the Israelites and had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.

notes.text: Hebrew metsora’at, traditionally “leprous.” The Hebrew term covers a range of skin diseases and is not limited to leprosy (Hansen’s disease).
Hebrew Adonai, “Lord,” a title of respect, not the divine name. So also in verse 13.
Hebrew adam, “humankind” or “a human being.”
Literally “send by the hand of whom you will send.”
The meaning of the name Aaron is uncertain; it may be of Egyptian origin.
Hebrew “you will be God to him.” Moses will give Aaron the message as God gives a message to a prophet. Compare 7:1.
Jether is a short form of Jethro; the Samaritan Pentateuch and several Hebrew manuscripts read “Jethro” here.

Hebrew hazaq, “to make strong” or “make firm.” Exodus uses three verbs for Pharaoh’s hardened heart: hazaq (“make strong,” as here), kaved (“make heavy,” first in 7:14), and qashah (“make hard,” first in 7:3). Sometimes God is the subject, sometimes Pharaoh hardens his own heart, and sometimes the text simply says that his heart was hardened.
Hebrew “met him.” The Hebrew does not say whether “him” is Moses or his son. The Septuagint reads “an angel of the Lord met him.”
Hebrew “his feet,” perhaps a polite way of referring to the genitals. Whose feet are meant, those of Moses, of the son, or of the one who attacked, is not stated.
Or “because of the circumcision.” The meaning of this very brief and ancient story is uncertain. Zipporah’s act seems to supply a missing circumcision and so to turn away the threat.

verses.text: Afterward Moses and Aaron went in and spoke to Pharaoh: “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel: ‘Send my people away, that they may celebrate a feast to me in the wilderness.’”
Pharaoh answered, “Who is Yahweh, that I should obey his voice and send Israel away? I do not know Yahweh, and I certainly will not send Israel away.”

They said, “The God of the Hebrews has encountered us. Let us go, we pray, a journey of three days into the wilderness and sacrifice to Yahweh our God, lest he strike us with pestilence or with the sword.”
The king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why do you draw the people away from their work? Go back to your burdens!”
Pharaoh also said, “Look, the people of the land are now many,{a} and you would make them rest from their labors!”
On that very day Pharaoh gave orders to the taskmasters over the people and to their foremen,{b}
“You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks, as in the past; let them go and collect straw for themselves.
But you are to require of them the same quota of bricks they made before. Do not reduce it, for they are lazy. That is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’
Let heavier work be laid on the men, so that they are kept busy with it and pay no attention to lying words.”
The people’s taskmasters and their foremen went out and spoke to the people: “Thus says Pharaoh: ‘I am not giving you straw.
You yourselves go and take straw wherever you can find it, but none of your work will be diminished.’”
So the people scattered throughout the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
The taskmasters kept pressing them, saying, “Finish your work, your daily quota, just as when there was straw.”
And the foremen of the Israelites, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and asked, “Why have you not completed your quota of bricks yesterday and today, as before?”
Then the foremen of the Israelites came and cried out to Pharaoh, “Why do you treat your servants this way?
No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are beaten, but the fault is with your own people.”{c}
He answered, “You are idle, you are idle! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to Yahweh.’
Now go and work. No straw will be given to you, but you must still deliver the full quota of bricks.”
The foremen of the Israelites saw that they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks.”
As they left Pharaoh’s presence, they encountered Moses and Aaron standing in their path to meet them.
They said to them, “May Yahweh look upon you and judge you, for you have made our scent foul in the eyes of Pharaoh and of his servants, putting a sword in their hands to kill us.”
Then Moses turned to Yahweh and said, “Lord,{d} why have you brought trouble on this people? Why did you ever send me?
From the time I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has dealt badly with this people, and you have not delivered your people at all.”

notes.text: The Samaritan Pentateuch reads “now they are more numerous than the people of the land.”
Hebrew shoterim, officials or scribes, here Israelites appointed over their own people (verse 14).
The Hebrew is difficult, literally “and your people sin.” The Septuagint reads “you wrong your people.”
Hebrew Adonai.

verses.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. Under a mighty hand he will let them go; under a mighty hand he will drive them out of his land.”
God spoke to Moses and said to him, “I am Yahweh.
I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Shaddai,{a} but I was not known to them by my name Yahweh.{b}
I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners.
Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are holding in slavery, and I have remembered my covenant.

Therefore say to the Israelites, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from beneath the forced labor of the Egyptians; I will free you from their servitude, and I will redeem{c} you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment.
I will take you as my people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
I will lead you into the land that I swore{d} to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and I will give it to you for a possession. I am Yahweh.’”
Moses spoke thus to the Israelites, but they did not heed him on account of their anguish of spirit{e} and their hard bondage.
Then Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the Israelites go out of his land.”
Moses spoke before Yahweh, saying, “See, the Israelites have not heeded me; how then will Pharaoh heed me, since my lips are uncircumcised?”{f}
Yet Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge concerning the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These are the heads of their fathers’ houses. The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon.
These are the names of Levi’s sons, by their generations: Gershon,{g} Kohath, and Merari. Levi’s lifetime was 137 years.
The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath’s lifetime was 133 years.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations.
Amram took Jochebed,{h} his father’s sister,{i} as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses.{j} Amram’s lifetime was 137 years.{k}
The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Aaron married Elisheba,{l} daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar,{m} and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites.
Eleazar, Aaron’s son, married one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas.{n} These are the heads of the fathers’ houses of the Levites by their clans.
These are the same Aaron and Moses to whom Yahweh said, “Bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.”{o}
It was these who spoke to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, in order to bring the Israelites out of Egypt—this Moses and this Aaron.
On the day when Yahweh spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
Yahweh said to Moses, “I am Yahweh. Tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything that I tell you.”
But Moses said before Yahweh, “Look, I have uncircumcised lips. How then will Pharaoh listen to me?”

notes.text: El Shaddai is traditionally translated “God Almighty,” following the Septuagint of some books and the Latin Vulgate (omnipotens). Its original meaning is uncertain; suggestions include “God of the mountain,” “God of the fields,” and “God who is sufficient.” It is the name by which God made himself known to Abraham in Genesis 17:1. The Septuagint here reads “being their God.”

Or as a question, “did I not make myself known to them?” The name Yahweh appears often in Genesis, so the point is probably that the patriarchs did not yet know God in the full sense of this name, as the one who keeps his promises by acts of deliverance.
Hebrew ga’al, to act as a kinsman-redeemer, a relative who buys back a family member from slavery or restores lost family property.
Literally “I lifted my hand,” a gesture of swearing an oath.
Hebrew “shortness of spirit,” that is, discouragement or impatience.
That is, lips unfit for speaking, as a closed or unready organ. Compare 4:10.
Gershon (or Gershom) probably sounds like garash, “drive out.” He is a different person from Moses’ son Gershom (2:22).
Jochebed probably means “Yahweh is glory”; it is the first personal name in the Bible built on the name Yahweh.
Hebrew dodah, “father’s sister” or “aunt.” The Septuagint and the Vulgate read “his father’s brother’s daughter,” that is, his cousin, perhaps to avoid a marriage later forbidden in Leviticus 18:12.
The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint add “and Miriam their sister.”
The Septuagint (Vaticanus) reads 132 years, and Codex Alexandrinus 136.
Elisheba means “my God is fullness” or “my God has sworn.” The same name appears in the New Testament as Elizabeth.
Eleazar means “God has helped.”
Phinehas is an Egyptian name meaning “the Nubian.”
Hebrew tsava’ot, “armies” or “hosts,” the same word as in the title “Yahweh of Armies.” Israel leaves Egypt organized like an army.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “See, I have made you like God{a} to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet.
You are to speak everything I command you, and your brother Aaron is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go out of his land.
I will harden{b} Pharaoh’s heart, and I will make my signs and my wonders many in the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my divisions, my people the Israelites, out of the land of Egypt with great acts of judgment.
The Egyptians will know that I am Yahweh when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them.”
Moses and Aaron did so; just as Yahweh commanded them, so they did.
Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.
Yahweh said to Moses and Aaron,
“When Pharaoh says to you, ‘Perform a wonder,’ then say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh,’ and it will become a serpent.”{c}
So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and did just as Yahweh had commanded. Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.
Pharaoh, for his part, summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and the magicians{d} of Egypt did likewise with their enchantments.
Each one threw down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron’s staff swallowed up their staffs.
Yet Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as Yahweh had said.
Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is stubborn;{e} he refuses to let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning, when he goes out to the water. Station yourself at the edge of the Nile to meet him, and take in your hand the staff that was changed into a snake.
Tell him, ‘Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to you with this message: “Send my people away, that they may serve me in the wilderness.” And see, until now you have not obeyed.
This is what Yahweh says: “By this you will know that I am Yahweh: I will strike the water in the Nile with the staff that is in my hand, and it will turn into blood.
The fish in the Nile will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will not be able to drink from the Nile’s water.”’”{f}

Yahweh said to Moses, “Say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, their ponds, and all their pools of water, so that they become blood.’ There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and of stone.”

Moses and Aaron did so, as Yahweh had commanded. Lifting up the staff, he struck the waters of the Nile before the eyes of Pharaoh and of his servants, and all the waters of the river were changed to blood.
The fish that were in the river died, and the river stank, and the Egyptians could not drink the Nile’s water; and there was blood in every part of the land of Egypt.
But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as Yahweh had said.
Pharaoh turned and went back to his house, and did not lay even this to heart.
All the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink the water of the Nile.
Seven full days passed after Yahweh had struck the Nile.

notes.text: Hebrew elohim, “God” or “a god.” Moses will speak with divine authority before Pharaoh, and Aaron will speak for him as a prophet speaks for God (compare 4:16).
Hebrew qashah, “make hard” or “make stubborn.” See the note at 4:21.
Hebrew tannin, a different word from the “snake” (nahash) of 4:3. It can mean a large serpent or a sea creature such as a crocodile.
Hebrew hartummim, a word borrowed from Egyptian, meaning priests skilled in sacred writings and magic. Jewish tradition gives the names of two of them as Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8).
Hebrew kaved, “heavy.” See the note at 4:21. In Egyptian belief the heart of the dead was weighed against a feather, and a heavy heart was a guilty one.

Throughout the plague accounts (chapters 7–11), the Samaritan Pentateuch adds passages that repeat God’s commands in full as Moses and Aaron carry them out, or that report Moses’ words to Pharaoh before each plague. Similar expansions appear in a Dead Sea Scroll of Exodus written in the old Hebrew script. This translation follows the shorter Masoretic Text.

verses.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses,{a} “Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, ‘This is what Yahweh says: “Let my people go, so that they may serve me.
If you refuse to let them go, I will strike your whole territory with frogs.

The Nile will swarm with frogs. They will come up into your house, into your bedroom and onto your bed, into the houses of your servants and onto your people, into your ovens and into your kneading bowls.
The frogs will come up on you, on your people, and on all your servants.”’”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Say to Aaron: ‘Reach out your hand with the staff above the streams, the canals, and the pools, so that frogs come up upon Egypt’s land.’”
So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs{b} came up and covered the land of Egypt.
The magicians did likewise with their enchantments and brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, “Pray to Yahweh to take the frogs away from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to Yahweh.”

Moses said to Pharaoh, “You may have the honor over me:{c} for when shall I pray for you, for your servants, and for your people, that the frogs be removed from you and your houses and remain only in the Nile?”
He said, “Tomorrow.” Moses said, “It will be as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like Yahweh our God.
The frogs will go away from you and your houses, your servants and your people; only in the Nile will they be left.”
Then Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to Yahweh about the frogs he had brought on Pharaoh.
Yahweh did according to Moses’ word, and the frogs died out of the houses, the courtyards, and the fields.
They piled them up in heaps, and the land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he made his heart stubborn and did not listen to them, just as Yahweh had said.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Extend your staff and hit the dust of the earth, that it may turn into gnats{d} in every part of the land of Egypt.’”
They did so: Aaron held out his hand with his staff and hit the dust of the earth, and gnats came upon man and beast. All the dust of the earth turned into gnats in the whole land of Egypt.
The magicians tried with their enchantments to bring forth gnats, but they were unable; and the gnats remained on man and beast.
Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as Yahweh had said.
Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh as he goes out to the water. Say to him, ‘This is what Yahweh says: “Let my people go, so that they may serve me.

If you will not let my people go, I will send swarms of flies{e} on you, on your servants, on your people, and into your houses. The houses of the Egyptians will be full of swarms of flies, and so will the ground they stand on.
On that day I will make a distinction regarding the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so there will be no swarm of flies there, that you may know that I, Yahweh, am in the midst of the land.{f}
I will put a division{g} between my people and your people. This sign will happen tomorrow.”’”
Yahweh did so. Thick swarms of flies entered Pharaoh’s house and the houses of his servants, and in all the land of Egypt the country was devastated by the flies.
Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, “Go, sacrifice to your God within the land.”

But Moses said, “It would not be right to do so, for the sacrifices we offer to Yahweh our God are detestable to the Egyptians. If we offer sacrifices detestable to the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us?
We must go a three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to Yahweh our God, as he tells us.”
Pharaoh said, “I will release you, and you may sacrifice to Yahweh your God in the wilderness; only do not go very far. Make entreaty for me.”

Moses said, “As soon as I go out from you, I will pray to Yahweh, and tomorrow the swarms of flies will depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people. Only let Pharaoh not deal falsely again by not letting the people go to sacrifice to Yahweh.”
So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to Yahweh.
Yahweh did as Moses asked and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; not one remained.
But Pharaoh made his heart stubborn this time also, and he did not let the people go.

notes.text: Verses 8:1–4 are numbered 7:26–29 in the Hebrew text, and verses 8:5–32 are numbered 8:1–28.
Hebrew “the frog,” used as a collective.
Literally “glorify yourself over me,” a courteous way of letting Pharaoh set the time.
Or “lice.” The exact insect is uncertain; the Septuagint reads “gnats” (skniphes).
Hebrew arov, “swarm” or “mixture.” The Septuagint takes it as “dog-flies.” Some Jewish interpreters understood it as a mixture of wild animals.
Or “I, Yahweh, am in the midst of the land.”

So the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate. The Hebrew reads pedut, “redemption,” which may be a copying error for pelut, “separation,” or may mean “I will set redemption between my people and your people.”

verses.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘This is what Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, says: “Let my people go, so that they may serve me.
For if you refuse to let them go and still hold on to them,
the hand of Yahweh will fall with a very heavy pestilence upon your livestock in the field: upon the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the cattle, and the sheep.
Yahweh will separate the livestock of Israel from the livestock of Egypt, and nothing belonging to the Israelites will die.”’”
Yahweh set a time, saying, “Tomorrow Yahweh will do this thing in the land.”
On the next day Yahweh did this. All the livestock of Egypt died,{a} yet of the Israelites’ livestock not a single one died.
Pharaoh sent men, and they found that not even one of Israel’s livestock was dead. Yet Pharaoh’s heart remained stubborn, and he did not release the people.
Yahweh said to Moses and Aaron, “Fill your hands with soot from a furnace, and let Moses toss it toward the sky before Pharaoh’s eyes.
It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt and will cause boils breaking out in sores on people and animals throughout all the land of Egypt.”
They took soot from the furnace and stood in Pharaoh’s presence; Moses tossed it toward the sky, and it became festering boils breaking out on man and beast.
The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils were on the magicians and on all the Egyptians.
But Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not listen to them, just as Yahweh had told Moses.
Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Rise early in the morning, stand before Pharaoh, and tell him, ‘This is what Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, says: “Let my people go, so that they may serve me.
For this time I will send all my plagues upon your heart,{b} upon your servants, and upon your people, so that you may know that there is no one like me in all the earth.
For by now I could have put out my hand and smitten you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth.
Yet for this very reason I have kept you standing:{c} to show you my power, and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.
You still exalt yourself against my people and will not let them go.
Tomorrow about this time I will rain down a very heavy hail, the like of which has not been in Egypt since the day it was founded until now.

Now therefore send and bring your livestock and all that you have in the field to safety. Every person and animal that is found in the field and not brought home will die when the hail comes down on them.”’”
Pharaoh’s servants who feared the word of Yahweh gathered their servants and livestock into houses.
But whoever did not take the word of Yahweh to heart left his servants and his livestock in the field.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Raise your hand toward the heavens, that hail may fall on the entire land of Egypt—upon man and beast and every plant of the field in the land of Egypt.”
Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky, and Yahweh sent thunder{d} and hail, and fire came down to the earth. Yahweh rained hail on the land of Egypt.
The hail fell, and fire flared up amid the hail—hail so very heavy that the like of it had not been seen in the whole land of Egypt since it became a nation.
Throughout the land of Egypt the hail beat down all that was in the open country, man and beast alike; it also beat down every plant of the field and broke every tree in the field.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites were, was there no hail.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, “I have sinned this time; Yahweh is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.
Pray to Yahweh, for there has been enough of God’s thunder{e} and hail. I will let you go; you need stay no longer.”

Moses said to him, “As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will spread out my hands to Yahweh. The thunder will stop, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth belongs to Yahweh.
But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear Yahweh God.”{f}
(The barley and the flax were destroyed, because the barley had come into ear while the flax was budding.
But the wheat and the spelt{g} were not struck down, for they ripen later.)
So Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh and spread out his hands to Yahweh. The thunder and the hail stopped, and the rain no longer poured on the earth.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned again, making his heart stubborn—he and his servants.
So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not let the Israelites go, just as Yahweh had said through Moses.

notes.text: That is, all the livestock in the field (verse 3). Livestock are again mentioned in 9:19–21 and 9:25, probably animals that had been sheltered or acquired since.
Or “against you yourself.” The Hebrew “upon your heart” may refer to the plagues’ effect on Pharaoh’s will.
Or “I have kept you alive” or “I have raised you up.” Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:17.
Hebrew “voices,” a common way of describing thunder. So also in verses 28, 29, 33, and 34.
Hebrew “voices of God,” or “mighty thunder.”
The full title “Yahweh God,” so frequent in Genesis 2–3, is rare elsewhere in the Pentateuch. The Septuagint reads “the Lord.”
Or “emmer,” an ancient variety of wheat.

verses.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh, for I have made his heart and the hearts of his servants stubborn, so that I may show these signs of mine among them,
and that you may tell your son and your grandson how severely I dealt with the Egyptians, and the signs that I performed among them, so that you will know that I am Yahweh.”

So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, “This is what Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, so that they may serve me.
For if you refuse to let my people go, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your territory.
They will cover the face of the land, so that no one can see the land. They will eat what is left to you after the hail, and they will eat every tree of yours that grows in the field.

They will fill your houses, and the houses of all your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians, as neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have ever seen since they were on the earth, down to this day.’” Then he turned and left Pharaoh’s presence.
Pharaoh’s servants said to him, “How long will this fellow be a trap for us? Release the men, that they may serve Yahweh their God. Have you not yet realized that Egypt is destroyed?”
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, and he said to them, “Go, serve Yahweh your God. But who exactly is going?”
Moses said, “We will go with our young and our old; with our sons and our daughters, with our sheep and our cattle we will go, for we have a festival of Yahweh.”
He said to them, “May Yahweh be with you if I ever let you go with your little ones!{a} Look, you clearly have evil in mind.
No! Go, you men, and serve Yahweh, for that is what you want.” And they were thrown out of Pharaoh’s presence.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Hold out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, that they may come up over the land of Egypt and devour all the plants of the land, everything the hail has left.”
So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and Yahweh drove an east wind over the land all that day and all that night. When it was morning, the east wind had brought the locusts.
The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled on the whole territory of Egypt in very great numbers. Never before had there been such a swarm of locusts, nor will there ever be again.

They covered the surface of the whole land, so that the land was darkened. They ate every plant of the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Nothing green remained, neither tree nor plant of the field, in all the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh hurriedly called Moses and Aaron and said, “I have sinned against Yahweh your God and against you.
So now, please pardon my sin this once only, and entreat Yahweh your God to take this death away from me.”
So he went out from Pharaoh and prayed to Yahweh.
Yahweh shifted the wind to an extremely strong west wind,{b} which lifted up the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea.{c} Not one locust remained anywhere within Egypt’s territory.
But Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the Israelites go.
Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, so that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness that can be felt.”
So Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt for three days.
One could not see another, and for three days no one got up from where he was; but all the Israelites had light in their dwellings.
Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, “Go, serve Yahweh. Only let your flocks and your herds stay behind. Even your little ones may go with you.”
Moses said, “You yourself must also supply{d} us with sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may offer them to Yahweh our God.

Our livestock too will go with us; we will leave not even a hoof behind, since we must choose some of them for the service of Yahweh our God, and we cannot know what we shall use to serve Yahweh until we get there.”
But Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was not willing to let them go.
Pharaoh said to him, “Get out of my sight! Take care not to appear before me again; for on the day you see my face you will die.”
Moses replied, “You have spoken rightly. I will never see your face again.”

notes.text: Pharaoh’s words are sarcastic: “May Yahweh be with you just as surely as I will let you go with your little ones.”
Hebrew “a sea wind,” that is, a wind from the Mediterranean Sea, to the west of Egypt.

Hebrew yam suf, literally “Sea of Reeds.” The Septuagint calls it the “Red Sea,” and the name is used in the Bible both for the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba, arms of the Red Sea, and perhaps for marshy lakes near the Isthmus of Suez. The exact place of Israel’s crossing (chapter 14) is uncertain.
Hebrew “give into our hand.”

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “I will bring one more plague on Pharaoh and on Egypt; afterward he will send you away from here. When he sends you away, he will drive you out altogether.
Tell the people, please, that each man is to ask of his neighbor and each woman of hers for silver articles and gold articles.”
Yahweh gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh’s servants and in the sight of the people.
Moses said, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘About midnight I will go out through the midst of Egypt.
Every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall perish, from the firstborn of Pharaoh sitting on his throne to the firstborn of the slave girl at the millstones, and all the firstborn of the cattle.
There will be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been and never will be again.
But among all the Israelites no dog will so much as growl,{a} whether at man or beast, so that you may know that Yahweh distinguishes between Egypt and Israel.’
All these servants of yours will come down to me and bow down to me, saying, ‘Go out, you and all the people who follow you.’ After that I will go out.” And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.
Yahweh had said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.”
Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the Israelites go out of his land.

notes.text: Hebrew “not a dog will sharpen its tongue.”

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,
“This month shall be the head of months for you; it is the first of the months of the year for you, in March–April.{a}
Tell the whole congregation of Israel: On the tenth day of this month (in March–April) each man is to take a lamb{b} for his family, a lamb for each household.

If a household is too small for a whole lamb, then he and the neighbor next to his house shall share one, in proportion to the number of persons; you shall apportion the lamb according to what each can eat.
Your lamb must be without defect, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats.
You are to keep it until the fourteenth day of this month (in March–April). Then the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel is to slaughter it at twilight.{c}
They are to take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.
They are to eat the meat that same night, roasted over the fire. They are to eat it with unleavened bread{d} and bitter herbs.
Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted over the fire, its head with its legs and its inner parts.
Do not leave any of it until morning. Whatever remains of it until morning you are to burn with fire.
In this way you shall eat it: your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it hurriedly. It is Yahweh’s Passover.{e}

For on that night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both people and animals, and on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments. I am Yahweh.
The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are. When I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will come upon you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.
“This day shall be a remembrance for you, and you shall celebrate it as a feast to Yahweh. Throughout your generations you shall observe it as an everlasting statute.

Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; on the very first day you shall clear out leaven from your houses, for anyone who eats leavened bread from the first day through the seventh, that person shall be cut off from Israel.

On the first day there shall be a holy convocation for you, and on the seventh day another holy convocation. No work shall be done in them, except what every person needs to eat; that alone may be prepared by you.
You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt. So you shall keep this day in all your generations, as an everlasting ordinance.
In the first month (March–April),{f} on the fourteenth day of the month, in the evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the month in the evening.
Seven days long no leaven may be found in your houses; for anyone who eats what is leavened, that person shall be cut off from the community of Israel, whether a sojourner or one born in the land.
You are not to eat anything leavened. In all your dwellings you are to eat unleavened bread.”
Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, “Go, select lambs for yourselves according to your families, and slaughter the Passover lamb.

You shall take a bunch of hyssop,{g} dip it in the blood in the basin,{h} and strike the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood from the basin; and none of you shall go out through the door of his house until morning.

For Yahweh will pass through to strike the Egyptians. When he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, Yahweh will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you.
You are to observe this as a statute for you and for your children forever.
When you come to the land that Yahweh will give you, as he has promised, you are to keep this service.
And when your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’

you shall say, ‘It is the sacrifice of Yahweh’s Passover, for he passed over the homes of the Israelites in Egypt when he struck down the Egyptians but delivered our households.’” Then the people bowed their heads and worshiped.
The Israelites departed and did it; as Yahweh had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.

At midnight Yahweh struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon,{i} and all the firstborn of the livestock.
Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians, and there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead.
Then he called Moses and Aaron by night and said, “Rise up, go out from among my people, both you and the Israelites. Go, serve Yahweh, as you have said.
Take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and go. And bless me also.”
The Egyptians urged the people to hurry and send them out of the land, for they said, “We will all be dead.”
So the people took their dough before it was leavened, with their kneading bowls bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders.
The Israelites had done as Moses said; they had asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and articles of gold, and for clothing.
Yahweh had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they gave them what they asked. So they plundered the Egyptians.
The Israelites set out from Rameses to Succoth,{j} about 600,000 men on foot,{k} besides children.
A mixed multitude{l} went up with them as well, along with flocks and herds, and a very large number of livestock.

From the dough that they had brought out of Egypt they baked cakes of unleavened bread, for it had not risen; they had been expelled from Egypt and were unable to delay, and they had made no provisions for themselves.
The time that the Israelites lived in Egypt{m} was 430 years.
And it came about at the end of 430 years, on that very day, that all the hosts of Yahweh went out from the land of Egypt.
It was a night of watching by Yahweh, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. This same night is a night of watching for Yahweh by all the Israelites throughout their generations.
Yahweh said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the statute of the Passover: no foreigner is to eat of it.
But any man’s slave who has been bought for money may eat of it after you have circumcised him.
No temporary resident or hired worker may eat of it.
It must be eaten within one house; none of the flesh may be taken outside the house, and you must not break any bone of it.{n}
The whole congregation of Israel is to keep it.

If a foreigner living among you wants to keep the Passover to Yahweh, all his males must be circumcised, and then he may come near and keep it. He will be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person may eat of it.
There is to be one law for the native and for the foreigner who lives among you.”
All the Israelites did so; just as Yahweh had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.
On that very day Yahweh brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.

notes.text: Hebrew “the first month.” This month, called Abib in the early sources (13:4) and later Nisan, begins the spring-start religious calendar. Because the Hebrew months were lunar, each overlaps two of our months, and the exact dates varied from year to year; the first month fell in March–April. The dates in verses 3, 6, and 18 are in this month.
Hebrew seh, a young animal of the flock, either a lamb or a young goat (verse 5).
Hebrew “between the two evenings,” understood either as between sunset and dark or as between midafternoon and sunset.
Hebrew matsot, flat bread made without yeast or leaven.
Hebrew pesah. The name is explained in verses 13, 23, and 27 by the verb pasah, “to pass over,” or perhaps “to protect, hover over.”
Hebrew “In the first month.” See the note at verse 2.
Hyssop is probably the plant now called Syrian marjoram (Origanum syriacum), whose hairy branches hold liquid well.
Or “on the threshold.” The Hebrew word saf can mean either.
Hebrew “the house of the pit.”
Rameses was the store city of 1:11, in the eastern Nile Delta. Succoth, meaning “booths,” is probably Egyptian Tjeku, in the Wadi Tumilat.
The Hebrew word elef, “thousand,” may in some lists mean a clan or military unit, so the number of people intended is debated.
Hebrew erev rav, people of other nations who joined Israel.

The Samaritan Pentateuch reads “in the land of Canaan and in the land of Egypt,” and the Septuagint reads “in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan.” Those readings count the 430 years from Abraham’s entry into Canaan, as Paul does in Galatians 3:17. Compare Genesis 15:13, which gives a round 400 years for the oppression.
John 19:36 applies this to Jesus.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Set apart for me every firstborn; whatever first opens the womb among the Israelites, of man and of beast, belongs to me.”

Moses said to the people, “Remember this day on which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by strength of hand Yahweh brought you out from this place. No leavened bread is to be eaten.
Today, in the month of Abib (March–April),{a} you are going out.

When Yahweh brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you are to keep this service in this month.
For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there is to be a festival to Yahweh.
Unleavened bread is to be eaten for the seven days. No leavened bread is to be seen with you, and no leaven is to be seen with you in all your territory.
You shall tell your son on that day, ‘This is on account of what Yahweh did for me when I came out of Egypt.’
It shall be for you as a sign upon your hand and as a memorial between your eyes,{b} that the law of Yahweh may be on your lips; for Yahweh brought you out of Egypt with a mighty hand.
You are to keep this statute at its appointed time from year to year.
“When Yahweh brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and to your fathers, and gives it to you,
you are to set apart to Yahweh all that first opens the womb. Every firstborn male of your livestock belongs to Yahweh.
Every firstborn donkey you shall redeem with a lamb; if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck. And every firstborn of your sons you shall redeem.
When your son asks you later, ‘What is this?’ you shall answer him, ‘By the strength of his hand Yahweh brought us out from Egypt, from the house of slavery.

For when Pharaoh was obstinate about sending us away, Yahweh slew every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of beast. Therefore I sacrifice to Yahweh all the males that open the womb, but every firstborn of my sons I redeem.’
It will be a sign on your hand and a symbol{c} between your eyes, for by strength of hand Yahweh brought us out of Egypt.”

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by the road to the land of the Philistines, although that was nearer. For God said, “The people may change their minds when they see war, and return to Egypt.”
God took the people around by the wilderness road to the Red Sea; the Israelites left the land of Egypt armed for battle.{d}
Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the Israelites solemnly swear, saying, “God will surely take note of you, and then you must carry my bones up from here with you.”{e}
They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness.
Yahweh was going before them in the daytime in a pillar of cloud to guide them on the road, and at night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so that they might travel day and night.
He did not remove the pillar of cloud by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, from its place before the people.

notes.text: Abib means “ears of grain,” the month of the barley harvest. It was the first month of the spring-start religious calendar (12:2), falling in March–April, and was later called Nisan.
That is, on the forehead. Later Jewish practice fulfilled this literally with tefillin (phylacteries), small boxes containing passages of the law.
Hebrew totafot, a band or emblem worn on the forehead.
Hebrew hamushim, perhaps “arranged in ranks” or “in groups of fifty.” The Septuagint reads “in the fifth generation.”
Genesis 50:25.

verses.text: Then Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Tell the Israelites to turn back and camp in front of Pi-hahiroth,{a} between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon. You are to camp facing it, by the sea.
Pharaoh will say of the Israelites, ‘They are wandering aimlessly in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.’
Then I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he pursues them; I will get glory{b} for myself over Pharaoh and over all his forces, and the Egyptians shall know that I am Yahweh.” So they did.

When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the hearts of Pharaoh and his servants were changed toward the people, and they said, “What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?”
So he harnessed his chariot and took his army with him.
He took six hundred select chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers{c} over all of them.
Yahweh hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the Israelites, while the Israelites were going out boldly.{d}
The Egyptians pursued them—every horse and chariot of Pharaoh, his cavalry, and his troops—and caught up with them camped at the sea, beside Pi-hahiroth, opposite Baal-zephon.
When Pharaoh came near, the Israelites lifted their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were advancing after them; and they were greatly afraid, and the Israelites cried out to Yahweh.
They said to Moses, “Is it because Egypt had no graves that you have taken us to die in the wilderness? Why have you treated us this way by bringing us out of Egypt?
Did we not say this to you in Egypt: ‘Let us be, so that we may serve the Egyptians’? For serving the Egyptians would have been better for us than dying in the wilderness.”
Moses said to the people, “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will accomplish for you today. For the Egyptians you see today you will never see again.
Yahweh will do battle for you, and you need only be silent.”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me? Tell the Israelites to go forward.
Lift up your staff, and hold out your hand over the sea and split it, so that the Israelites can walk into the midst of the sea on dry land.
And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they will go in after them, and I will gain glory over Pharaoh and all his army, his chariots, and his horsemen.
The Egyptians will know that I am Yahweh when I have gained glory over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.”
The angel of God, who went ahead of the camp of Israel, moved away and went behind them; and the pillar of cloud left its place in front and stood behind them,
and it came between the Egyptian camp and the camp of Israel. The cloud was there with the darkness, yet it lit the night;{e} so neither came near the other all night long.
Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
The Israelites went into the middle of the sea on dry ground, with the waters forming a wall for them on their right and on their left.
The Egyptians pursued and went in after them into the middle of the sea, all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.
Between about two and six in the morning,{f} Yahweh gazed down from the pillar of fire and cloud upon the army of the Egyptians and threw them into a panic.
He took off the wheels of their chariots,{g} so that they drove them with difficulty. The Egyptians said, “Let us run away from Israel, for Yahweh is fighting on their behalf against Egypt.”
Then Yahweh told Moses, “Reach your hand out over the sea, that the waters may return upon the Egyptians, on their chariots and on their horsemen.”
So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its normal flow. As the Egyptians fled before it, Yahweh shook off the Egyptians into the middle of the sea.
The waters flowed back and covered the chariots and the horsemen of all Pharaoh’s forces that had gone in after them into the sea; not a single one of them was left.
As for the Israelites, they went on dry land in the middle of the sea, and the waters were a wall to them on the right and on the left.
So Yahweh saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great power{h} that Yahweh used against the Egyptians, and the people feared Yahweh, and they believed in Yahweh and in his servant Moses.

notes.text: Pi-hahiroth may be Egyptian for “house of Hathor” or Hebrew for “mouth of the canals.” Migdol means “tower” or “fortress,” and Baal-zephon means “lord of the north,” the name of a Canaanite god given to a place. None of these sites has been identified with certainty.
Or “glorify myself,” “show my glory.” So also in verses 17 and 18.
Hebrew shalishim, perhaps “third men,” the third man in a chariot, or more generally high-ranking officers.
Hebrew “with a high hand,” that is, openly and defiantly.
The Hebrew is difficult. It may mean that the cloud brought darkness to the Egyptians and light to Israel. The Septuagint reads “and there was darkness and blackness, and the night passed.”
Hebrew “In the morning watch,” the last of the three watches into which the night was divided, from about 2 a.m. until about 6 a.m.
So the Hebrew, literally “he turned aside the wheels.” The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac read “he bound” or “clogged,” a difference of one letter.
Hebrew “the great hand.”

verses.text: Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to Yahweh, and said: “I will sing to Yahweh, for he is highly exalted;{a} horse and its rider{b} he has thrown into the sea.
Yah{c} is my strength and my song,{d} and he has become my salvation. This is my God, and I will praise him, my father’s God, and I will exalt him.
Yahweh is a warrior; Yahweh is his name.
Pharaoh’s chariots and his forces he hurled into the sea; the pick of his officers were sunk in the Red Sea.
The deeps cover them; they went down into the depths like a stone.
Your right hand, Yahweh, glorious in power, your right hand, Yahweh, shatters the enemy.
By the abundance of your majesty you throw down those who rise up against you; you let loose your wrath, and it devours them like stubble.
By the breath of your nostrils the waters were heaped together; the floods stood upright like a mound; the depths were frozen in the midst of the sea.
The enemy said, ‘I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the plunder; my desire will have its fill of them. I will draw my sword; my hand will destroy them.’
You blew with your breath; the sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who among the gods is like you, Yahweh? Who is like you, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, working wonders?
You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them.
In your loyal love{e} you led the people you redeemed; you guided them in your strength to your holy abode.
Nations have heard and shudder; pangs have taken hold of those who live in Philistia.
Now the chiefs of Edom are terrified; trembling grips the leaders{f} of Moab; all who live in Canaan have melted away.
Fear and dread fall upon them; by the might of your arm they are motionless as stone, until your people cross over, Yahweh, until the people you have acquired go across.{g}
You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, the place, Yahweh, which you have made for your dwelling, the sanctuary, Lord,{h} which your hands have established.
Yahweh will reign forever and ever.”
For when Pharaoh’s horses with his chariots and his horsemen went into the sea, Yahweh brought back the waters of the sea upon them, but the Israelites walked on dry ground in the middle of the sea.
Then Miriam{i} the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dancing.
Miriam sang to them: “Sing to Yahweh, for he is highly exalted; horse and its rider he has thrown into the sea.”
Then Moses had Israel depart from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur;{j} they traveled three days in the wilderness and found no water.
They arrived at Marah but could not drink the water there, because it was bitter; therefore its name was called Marah.{k}
The people grumbled against Moses, saying, “What are we to drink?”

Moses cried to Yahweh, and Yahweh showed him a piece of wood.{l} He cast it into the water, and the water became sweet. There Yahweh{m} established for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he tested them.

He said, “If you will diligently obey the voice of Yahweh your God, doing what is right in his eyes, giving ear to his commandments, and keeping all his statutes, I will lay on you none of the sicknesses that I laid on the Egyptians; for I am Yahweh, your healer.”{n}
Then they came to Elim,{o} where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the water.

notes.text: Literally “for he has risen up proudly,” or “gloriously triumphed.” The Hebrew repeats the verb for emphasis.
Or “its chariot driver.”
Yah is a short form of Yahweh, appearing first here. It is familiar from the word hallelujah, “praise Yah.”
Or “my might.” Verse 2a is repeated in Isaiah 12:2 and Psalm 118:14.
Hebrew hesed, the faithful, steadfast love that belongs to a covenant relationship.
Hebrew “rams,” a figure for chiefs or strong men.
Or “created.”
Hebrew Adonai. Many Hebrew manuscripts and the Samaritan Pentateuch read “Yahweh.”
The meaning of the name Miriam is uncertain; suggestions include “bitter,” “beloved” (from Egyptian), and “rebellious.” The Greek form of the name is Mariam, the name Mary in the New Testament.
Shur means “wall,” perhaps named after a line of Egyptian border fortifications.
Marah means “bitter.”
Or “a tree.”
Hebrew “he.”
Hebrew Yahweh rofe’ekha. Some later writers turned this phrase into the compound name “Yahweh Rophe,” “Yahweh who heals.”
Elim means “large trees” or “terebinths.”

verses.text: They set out from Elim, and the whole congregation of the Israelites came to the wilderness of Sin,{a} which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month (in April–May){b} after they had come out of the land of Egypt.
The whole congregation of the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness.

The Israelites said to them, “Would that we had died by Yahweh’s hand in the land of Egypt, where we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full! For you have led us out into this wilderness to let this entire assembly die of hunger.”

Yahweh said to Moses, “See, I will soon rain bread from heaven for you; the people shall go out and gather each day’s portion on its day, that I may test them to see whether they will walk in my law or not.
On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather on other days.”
Moses and Aaron told all the Israelites, “In the evening you will know that it is Yahweh who brought you out of the land of Egypt,
and in the morning you will see the glory of Yahweh, because he has heard your grumbling against Yahweh. For what are we, that you grumble against us?”

Moses said, “Yahweh will give you meat to eat in the evening and in the morning bread to the full, because Yahweh has heard your grumbling that you make against him. Who are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against Yahweh.”
Then Moses said to Aaron, “Say to the whole congregation of the Israelites, ‘Come near before Yahweh, for he has heard your grumbling.’”
While Aaron was speaking to the whole community of the Israelites, they turned toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of Yahweh appeared in the cloud.
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,

“I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Speak to them and say, ‘At twilight{c} you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am Yahweh your God.’”
In the evening quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp.
When the layer of dew had gone up, there on the surface of the wilderness was something fine and flaky, fine as frost on the ground.
When the Israelites saw it, they said to one another, “What is it?”{d} For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them, “It is the bread that Yahweh has given you to eat.

This is what Yahweh has commanded: ‘Each of you is to gather as much of it as he can eat. You are to take about 2 quarts{e} for each person, according to the number of persons; each of you is to take it for those in his tent.’”
The Israelites did so. They gathered, some more and some less.
But when they measured it out,{f} whoever had gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever had gathered little had no lack. Each had gathered as much as he could eat.
Moses said to them, “No one is to leave any of it until morning.”
But they did not listen to Moses. Some of them left part of it until morning, and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them.
They gathered it every morning, each according to what he needed to eat; and when the sun grew hot, it melted away.
On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, about 4 quarts{g} for each person. When all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses,

he said to them, “This is what Yahweh commanded: ‘Tomorrow is a Sabbath of complete rest, a holy Sabbath{h} to Yahweh. What you will bake, bake; and what you will boil, boil; and all the remainder lay up for yourselves to keep until morning.’”
They laid it up until morning, as Moses had ordered; and it did not smell foul, and no worm was in it.
Moses said, “Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to Yahweh. Today you will not find it in the field.
For six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is the Sabbath, there will be none.”
On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none.
Then Yahweh said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?
See, Yahweh has given you the Sabbath; that is why on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Each of you is to stay where he is; no one is to go out of his place on the seventh day.”
So the people rested on the seventh day.
The house of Israel named it manna.{i} It was like coriander seed, white, and its taste was like wafers made with honey.

Moses said, “This is what Yahweh has commanded: ‘Let about 2 quarts{j} of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’”
Moses told Aaron, “Take one jar and put in it about 2 quarts of manna, and set it before Yahweh to be preserved for your generations.”
As Yahweh commanded Moses, so Aaron placed it before the testimony,{k} to be kept.
The Israelites ate the manna forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate the manna until they came to the border of the land of Canaan.
(The daily measure of about 2 quarts was one tenth of the standard dry measure of about three-fifths of a bushel.){l}

notes.text: Sin here is a place name, unrelated to the English word “sin.” It is probably related to the name Sinai.

Hebrew “on the fifteenth day of the second month,” counting from the spring new year (see the note at 12:2). The second month, later called Iyyar (Ziv in 1 Kings 6:1), fell in April–May. This was one month after the exodus (12:18).
Hebrew “Between the two evenings.” See the note at 12:6.
Hebrew man hu, “What is it?” The phrase explains the name manna (verse 31).
Hebrew “an omer.” An omer was about 2 dry quarts (about 2.2 liters). See verse 36.
Hebrew “when they measured it with the omer.”
Hebrew “two omers,” about 4 dry quarts (about 4.4 liters).
Hebrew shabbaton shabbat-qodesh, “a rest, a holy Sabbath.” The word Sabbath comes from shavat, “to stop” or “to rest.” This is the first time the word appears in the Bible.
Hebrew man, “What?” (see verse 15). Numbers 11:7–9 also describes it.
Hebrew “an omerful.” So also in verse 33.
That is, before the ark that would hold the tablets of the testimony (25:16, 21–22). The narrator speaks of the later practice.
