Hebrew “The omer is a tenth of the ephah.” The omer was about 2.2 liters (2 dry quarts), and the ephah about 22 liters (three-fifths of a bushel). Ancient standards varied.

verses.text: The whole congregation of the Israelites set out from the wilderness of Sin, traveling in stages at Yahweh’s command,{a} and camped at Rephidim.{b} But there was no water for the people to drink.
So the people quarreled with Moses and said, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test Yahweh?”
The people were thirsty there for water, and they grumbled against Moses, saying, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried out to Yahweh, “What am I to do with this people? Before long they will stone me.”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Go on ahead of the people and take with you some of the elders of Israel; and the staff with which you struck the Nile, take in your hand and go.
I will be standing there before you on the rock at Horeb; you shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it for the people to drink.” Moses did so before the eyes of the elders of Israel.
He named the place Massah and Meribah,{c} because of the quarreling of the Israelites, and because they tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us or not?”
Then Amalek{d} came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua,{e} “Choose men for us, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.”
Joshua did as Moses had told him, fighting against Amalek; and Moses, with Aaron and Hur,{f} climbed to the top of the hill.
As long as Moses kept his hand raised, Israel prevailed; but when he let his hand down, Amalek prevailed.
Moses’ hands became heavy, so they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat on it; and Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on each side, so that his hands remained steady until sunset.
And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.{g}
Yahweh said to Moses, “Write this in a book{h} as a reminder, and recite it to Joshua: I will utterly erase the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”
Moses built an altar and named it Yahweh Nissi,{i}
saying, “A hand upon the throne of Yah!{j} Yahweh will be at war with Amalek from generation to generation.”

notes.text: Hebrew “by the mouth of Yahweh.”
Rephidim perhaps means “resting places” or “supports.” Its location is uncertain.
Massah means “testing” and Meribah means “quarreling.”
Amalek, a desert people descended from Esau’s grandson Amalek (Genesis 36:12).
This is the first appearance of Joshua, Hebrew Yehoshua, “Yahweh saves.” His earlier name was Hoshea, “salvation” (Numbers 13:16). The Greek form of the name is Iesous, “Jesus.”
Hur perhaps means “child” or is of Egyptian origin, from the god Horus. Jewish tradition made him Miriam’s husband. See also 24:14.
Hebrew “by the mouth of the sword.”
Or “on a scroll.” Hebrew sefer, “a written document.”
Yahweh Nissi means “Yahweh is my banner.” A banner was a pole or standard raised as a rallying point in battle, recalling Moses’ raised staff.

The Hebrew is difficult. It may mean “a hand raised to the throne of Yah,” an oath, or, if kes (“throne”) is read as nes (“banner”), “a hand upon the banner of Yah,” matching the name Yahweh Nissi. The Septuagint reads “with a secret hand the Lord wars against Amalek.” On Yah, see the note at 15:2.

verses.text: Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses’ father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for his people Israel, how Yahweh had brought Israel out of Egypt.
Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, had taken Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after she had been sent away,{a}
along with her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom, for he said, “I have become a foreigner in a foreign land,”
and the name of the other was Eliezer,{b} for he said, “The God of my father was my help and rescued me from the sword of Pharaoh.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came with Moses’ sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness, where he was camped at the mountain of God.
He sent word to Moses,{c} “I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons with her.”
Moses went out to meet his father-in-law. He bowed down and kissed him, and they asked each other about their welfare, and they went into the tent.

Moses recounted to his father-in-law everything that Yahweh had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians on Israel’s account, all the hardship that had befallen them along the way, and how Yahweh had delivered them.
Jethro was glad because of all the good that Yahweh had done for Israel, since he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians.
Jethro said, “Blessed be Yahweh, who has rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh, who has rescued the people from under the hand of the Egyptians.
Now I know that Yahweh is greater than all gods, because of what came about when they acted insolently against the people.”{d}
Then Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law before God.
The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning until evening.

When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, with all the people standing around you from morning until evening?”
Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God.
When they have a dispute, it comes to me, and I judge between one person and another, and I make known the statutes of God and his laws.”
Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not good.
You will certainly wear yourself out, you and this people who are with you, for the work is too heavy for you; you are not able to do it by yourself.
Now listen to me; let me counsel you, and may God be with you. Be the people’s representative before God, and bring their cases to him.
Teach them the statutes and the laws, and make known to them the way in which they must walk and the work they must do.

Moreover you shall look out from among all the people capable men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them as rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

Let them judge the people at all times. Every major dispute they are to bring to you, but every minor dispute they may decide themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you.
If you do this, and God so commands you, then you will be able to endure, and all these people also will go to their place in peace.”
So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said.
Moses chose capable men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people, officers over thousands, officers over hundreds, officers over fifties, and officers over tens.{e}
They judged the people at all times. Any difficult case they brought to Moses, but every minor case they decided themselves.
Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own land.

notes.text: Hebrew shilluheha, “her sending away.” The text does not say when or why Moses sent her back; the last mention of her is 4:20–26.
Eliezer means “my God is help.”
So the Hebrew. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac read “Someone said to Moses, ‘Look, your father-in-law Jethro is coming to you.’”
The Hebrew of the last part of the verse is brief and difficult, literally “for in the thing in which they acted proudly against them.”
At this point the Samaritan Pentateuch adds a passage drawn from Deuteronomy 1:9–18, in which Moses describes the appointment of the judges in his own words.

verses.text: In the third month (in May–June){a} after the Israelites had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that very day,{b} they came into the wilderness of Sinai.
They set out from Rephidim, came into the wilderness of Sinai, and camped in the wilderness. Israel camped there in front of the mountain.
Moses went up to God, and Yahweh called to him from the mountain, saying, “This is what you are to say to the house of Jacob and tell the Israelites:
‘You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.
And now, if you will truly obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my own treasured possession{c} among all the peoples; for the whole earth is mine.
You will be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you are to speak to the Israelites.”
So Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that Yahweh had commanded him.
The whole people answered as one, “Everything that Yahweh has spoken we will do.” Then Moses reported the people’s words to Yahweh.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Look, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you and may also believe you forever.” Then Moses told the people’s words to Yahweh.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow. Let them wash their clothes
and be ready for the third day, for on the third day Yahweh will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.
You shall mark off a boundary for the people all around and say, ‘Beware of going up the mountain or touching its border; anyone who touches the mountain shall surely be put to death.
No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot with arrows; beast or man, he shall not live. When the ram’s horn gives a long blast, they may go up on the mountain.”{d}
Moses came down from the mountain to the people and sanctified the people, and they washed their garments.
He said to the people, “Be ready for the third day. Do not go near a woman.”
On the third day, as morning came, there were thunder and lightning, a dense cloud over the mountain, and a very loud trumpet blast, and all the people in the camp shuddered.
Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stationed themselves at the base of the mountain.
Mount Sinai was entirely in smoke, because Yahweh had descended upon it in fire; its smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain{e} shook violently.
As the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice.{f}
Yahweh came down on Mount Sinai, on the top of the mountain. Yahweh called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Go down and warn the people, so that they do not break through to Yahweh to look, and many of them perish.
Even the priests who come near to Yahweh must consecrate themselves, or Yahweh will break out against them.”
Moses said to Yahweh, “The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai, because you yourself charged us, ‘Mark off boundaries around the mountain and make it holy.’”
Yahweh said to him, “Go down, and then come up, you together with Aaron; but the priests and the people must not break through to come up to Yahweh, lest he burst out against them.”
So Moses went down to the people and told them.

notes.text: Hebrew “In the third month,” later called Sivan, counting from the spring new year (see the note at 12:2).
Literally “on this day,” probably the first day of the month, the new moon.
Hebrew segullah, a personal treasure, such as a king’s private property.
Hebrew yovel, “ram’s horn.” The trumpet (shofar) of verses 16 and 19 is a different word for a similar instrument.
The Septuagint and some Hebrew manuscripts read “the whole people.”
Or “in thunder.” The Hebrew word qol means both “voice” and “thunder.”

verses.text: Then God spoke all these words, saying,{a}
“I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
“You shall have no other gods before me.{b}
“You shall not make yourself a carved image,{c} nor any likeness of what is in the heavens above, or on the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth.

You shall not bow down to them nor serve them; for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God,{d} punishing the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, upon the third and upon the fourth generation of those who hate me,
but showing loyal love to thousands{e} of those who love me and keep my commandments.
“You shall not take up the name of Yahweh your God for emptiness,{f} for Yahweh will not leave unpunished anyone who takes up his name for emptiness.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
Six days you shall labor and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God: you shall do no work on it—you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor the sojourner within your gates.
For in six days Yahweh made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and everything in them, and he rested on the seventh day; this is why Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day and hallowed it.
“Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be long in the land that Yahweh your God is giving you.
“You shall not murder.{g}
“You shall not commit adultery.
“You shall not steal.
“You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s house; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”{h}
All the people saw the thunder and the lightning, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking. When the people saw it, they trembled and stood at a distance.
They said to Moses, “You speak to us, and we will hear; but let not God speak to us, lest we die.”
Moses said to the people, “Do not be afraid, for God has come to test you, and so that the fear of him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.”
So the people stood far off, but Moses approached the thick darkness where God was.{i}
Yahweh said to Moses, “This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘You yourselves have seen that I have spoken with you from heaven.
You shall not make alongside me gods of silver, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves.

You are to make for me an altar of earth and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings,{j} your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you.
If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it with hewn stones; for if you wield your chisel on it, you have profaned it.
And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, so that your nakedness may not be exposed on it.’

notes.text: The Ten Commandments, called in Hebrew “the ten words” (34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13), are given again in Deuteronomy 5:6–21 with some differences. Jewish and Christian traditions divide them in different ways.
Or “besides me,” or “in defiance of me.” Literally “before my face.”
Hebrew pesel, an idol carved from wood or stone, or cast in metal.
Hebrew El qanna, “a jealous God,” one who is zealous for an exclusive relationship, as a husband for his marriage. See 34:14, where Qanna is given as a name.
Or “to the thousandth generation,” in contrast with the third and fourth generation of verse 5. Compare Deuteronomy 7:9. On “loyal love,” see the note at 15:13.
Or “You shall not misuse the name” or “lift up the name … in vain.” The command forbids using God’s name for falsehood, such as false oaths, or for worthless ends.

Hebrew ratsah, unlawful killing. The word is not used for killing in war or for lawful execution. The Septuagint (Vaticanus) gives verses 13–15 in the order “You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not murder.”
After this verse the Samaritan Pentateuch adds a commandment, drawn from Deuteronomy 11:29–30 and 27:2–7, to build an altar on Mount Gerizim.
In verses 19–21 the Samaritan Pentateuch adds passages drawn from Deuteronomy 5:24–31 and 18:18–22, including the promise of a prophet like Moses.
Hebrew shelamim, offerings for fellowship, thanksgiving, or vows, shared by the worshiper, the priests, and God.

verses.text: “These are the rules{a} that you are to set before them.
“When you buy a Hebrew slave,{b} he is to serve six years, and in the seventh he is to go out free, without payment.
If he comes in single, he is to go out single. If he is married, his wife is to go out with him.
If his master gives him a wife, and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master’s, and he shall go out by himself.
But if the slave plainly says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,’
then his master shall bring him to God,{c} and shall bring him to the door or to the doorpost; and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him forever.
“When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she is not to go out as the male slaves do.

If she displeases her master, who had designated her for himself,{d} then he shall let her be redeemed. To sell her to a foreign people he shall have no power, seeing he has dealt deceitfully with her.
If he designates her for his son, he is to deal with her as with a daughter.
If he takes another wife for himself, he must not reduce her food, her clothing, or her marital rights.{e}
If he does not do these three things for her, she is to go out free, without payment of money.
“Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death.
But if he did not lie in wait for him, and God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.
But if a man acts willfully against his neighbor to kill him by cunning, you are to take him even from my altar, so that he may die.
“Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.
“Whoever kidnaps a man, whether he has sold him or he is still found in his possession, must surely be put to death.
“Whoever curses{f} his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.
“If men quarrel, and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist, and he does not die but keeps to his bed,
then if he gets up and walks around outside with his staff, the one who struck him will be free of liability. He must only pay for the loss of his time and see that he is fully healed.
“When a man strikes his male or female slave with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, the slave must be avenged.
Yet if the slave lives on a day or two, he shall not be avenged, for he is the owner’s money.{g}

“If men fight with one another and hurt a pregnant woman so that her children come out,{h} and yet no harm follows, he shall surely be fined, according to what the woman’s husband lays on him; and he shall pay as the judges determine.
But if there is serious injury, then you are to give life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.{i}
“When a man strikes the eye of his male or female slave and destroys it, he is to let the slave go free in compensation for the eye.
If he knocks out the tooth of his male or female slave, he is to let the slave go free in compensation for the tooth.
“If an ox gores a man or a woman so that either dies, the ox shall surely be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be free of blame.
But if the ox was accustomed to goring in time past, and its owner was warned but did not confine it, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death.
If a ransom is imposed on him, then he is to give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed on him.
Whether it gores a son or gores a daughter, it shall be done to him according to this same judgment.
If the ox gores a male or female slave, the owner is to give to their master about 12 ounces of silver,{j} and the ox is to be stoned.
“If a man opens a pit, or if a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls in,
the owner of the pit is to make it good. He is to pay money to its owner, and the dead animal will be his.
“When one man’s ox injures his neighbor’s ox so that it dies, they are to sell the live ox and divide its price, and they are also to divide the dead animal.
Or if it is known that the ox has been in the habit of goring in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he must surely repay ox for ox, and the dead animal will be his.

notes.text: Hebrew mishpatim, “judgments” or “ordinances,” case laws that apply the covenant. Chapters 21–23 are often called the Book of the Covenant (24:7).
Or “servant.” Hebrew eved means a slave or servant, including a person in debt service, as here, who serves for a limited term.
Or “to the judges.” Hebrew elohim may refer to God at the sanctuary or to judges acting in his name. So also in 22:8–9.
So the main Hebrew reading. The traditional Hebrew margin and the Samaritan Pentateuch read “so that he has not designated her.”
Or “her shelter” or “her ointment.” The Hebrew word onah occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain.
Or “treats with contempt.” Hebrew qillel, “make light of.”
Hebrew “for he is his money.”

That is, she gives birth prematurely, or perhaps miscarries. The phrase “no serious injury” (Hebrew ason, “harm”) may refer to the woman, the child, or both; interpreters differ. The Septuagint distinguishes a child born “not fully formed,” for which a fine is paid, from one “fully formed,” for which the penalty is life for life.
The principle of equal justice (lex talionis) set the limit of a penalty and was generally applied through monetary compensation.
Hebrew “thirty shekels of silver,” about 12 ounces (345 grams). Compare Zechariah 11:12–13 and Matthew 26:15.

verses.text: “If a man steals an ox or a sheep{a} and kills it or sells it, he shall pay back five oxen for the ox, and four sheep for the sheep.
If the thief is found breaking in, and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt on his account.
If the sun has risen on him, blood is due for him. He must make full restitution; and if he has nothing, he shall be sold for his theft.
If the stolen animal is found alive in his possession, whether ox or donkey or sheep, he is to repay double.

“When a man lets a field or vineyard be grazed over, or lets his animal loose and it grazes in another man’s field, he is to make restitution from the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.{b}
“If fire breaks out and spreads to thorns, and the shocks of grain, or the standing grain, or the field are consumed, he who kindled the fire shall surely make restitution.
“If a man gives money or articles to his neighbor for safekeeping, and it is stolen out of that man’s house, and the thief is caught, he shall pay back double.
If the thief is not found, the owner of the house is to come near to God{c} to show whether he has put his hand to his neighbor’s property.

For every kind of breach of trust, whether for ox, donkey, sheep, clothing, or any lost thing about which one says, ‘This is it,’ the cause of both parties shall come before God; whomever God condemns{d} shall pay double to his neighbor.
“When a man gives his neighbor a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any animal to keep, and it dies or is injured or is driven away, with no one seeing it,
an oath of Yahweh shall be between the two of them, whether he has put his hand to his neighbor’s goods; and its owner shall accept it, and he shall not make restitution.
But if it was actually stolen from him, he is to make restitution to its owner.
If it has been torn to pieces by a beast, let him bring it as evidence; he need not pay for what was torn.
“When a man borrows an animal from his neighbor, and it is injured or dies while its owner is not with it, he must make full restitution.
If its owner was with it, he does not have to make restitution. If it was hired, the hiring fee covers the loss.{e}
“If a man entices a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall certainly endow her to be his wife by paying the bride price.{f}
If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he is to pay money equal to the bride-price for virgins.
“You shall not let a sorceress live.
“Whoever lies with an animal must surely be put to death.
“Whoever sacrifices to any god other than Yahweh alone is to be devoted to destruction.{g}
“You shall not wrong a foreigner or oppress him, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.
You shall not mistreat any widow or orphan.
If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry,
and my anger will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives will become widows and your children orphans.
“If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not act like a moneylender to him; you shall not charge him interest.
If you take your neighbor’s garment in pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun sets,
for that is his only covering, it is his garment for his skin. In what shall he sleep? And when he cries to me, I will hear, for I am gracious.
“You shall not revile God,{h} nor curse a ruler of your people.
“You shall not hold back the first of your ripe harvest and of the overflow of your presses.{i} The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me.
You are to do the same with your oxen and your sheep. Seven days it is to be with its mother; on the eighth day you are to give it to me.
“You are to be holy people to me. Therefore you shall not eat any meat that is torn by beasts in the field; you are to throw it to the dogs.

notes.text: Verse 22:1 is numbered 21:37 in the Hebrew text, and verses 22:2–31 are numbered 22:1–30.

The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint have a longer text: “… he is to make restitution from his own field according to its yield. But if it grazes over the whole field, he is to make restitution from the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.”
Or “before the judges.” See the note at 21:6.
Or “whom the judges declare guilty.” The verb is plural, which may suggest judges acting for God.
Or “if it was hired, he must bear the loss of the hire.” The Hebrew is brief, literally “if it was hired, it came for its hire.”
Hebrew mohar, the payment a bridegroom gave to the bride’s family.
Hebrew herem, set apart irrevocably to God, which in the case of a person meant death.
Or “the judges.” Hebrew elohim. Paul quotes the second half of this verse in Acts 23:5.
The Hebrew is brief: “your fullness and your trickling,” that is, the first of the grain harvest and of the juice from the wine press and olive press.

verses.text: “You shall not spread a false report. Do not join hands with a wicked person to be a malicious witness.
You shall not follow a crowd in doing evil, nor shall you testify in a lawsuit siding with a crowd to pervert justice.
Nor shall you show partiality to a poor man in his lawsuit.
“If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you must take it back to him.
If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying down under its load, you shall not leave him alone with it; you must help him free it.{a}
“You shall not turn aside the justice owed to your poor in his dispute.
Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and the righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked.
You shall not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and subverts the cause of the righteous.
“You shall not oppress a stranger; you yourselves know the life{b} of a stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.
“For six years you are to sow your land and gather in its produce,

but in the seventh year you are to let it rest and lie fallow, so that the poor of your people may eat. What they leave, the wild animals may eat. You are to do the same with your vineyard and your olive grove.
For six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall cease, that your ox and your donkey may rest, and the female servant’s son and the resident alien may be refreshed.
Take heed to everything I have said to you; do not make mention of the names of other gods, nor let them be heard from your lips.
“You shall keep a feast to me three times in the year.

You are to keep the Festival of Unleavened Bread. For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time in the month of Abib (March–April),{c} for in it you came out of Egypt. No one is to appear before me empty-handed.

Also the Feast of Harvest,{d} the firstfruits of your labors, which you sow in the field; and the Feast of Ingathering{e} at the end of the year, when you gather in the produce of your labors from the field.
Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Lord Yahweh.{f}
“You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, and the fat of my festival sacrifice is not to remain until morning.
The best of the firstfruits of your ground you are to bring into the house of Yahweh your God. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.{g}
“Look, I am sending an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared.
Take heed before him and obey his voice; do not provoke him, for he will not forgive your transgressions, since my name is in him.
But if you carefully listen to his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.
For my angel will go before you and bring you to the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, and I will wipe them out.
You shall not bow down to their gods or serve them, nor do as they do, but you are to demolish them completely and break their sacred pillars in pieces.
You are to serve Yahweh your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you.
No woman will miscarry or be barren in your land; I will fulfill the number of your days.
“I will send my terror before you and throw into confusion all the people against whom you come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.
I will send the hornet{h} before you, which will drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites from before you.
I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate, and the beasts of the field multiply against you.
Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and take possession of the land.

I will set your border from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines,{i} and from the wilderness to the River,{j} for I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you will drive them out before you.
You shall make no covenant with them or with their gods.
They shall not dwell in your land, lest they cause you to sin against me; for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you.”

notes.text: The Hebrew is difficult; literally, “you shall cease from leaving it to him; you shall certainly loose it along with him.”
Hebrew nefesh, “soul,” “life,” or “inner feelings.”
Hebrew “the month of Abib.” See the note at 13:4.
That is, the wheat harvest in late spring, later called the Festival of Weeks (34:22) or Pentecost.
That is, the autumn harvest of fruit and olives, later called the Festival of Booths or Tabernacles.
Hebrew ha’adon YHWH, “the Lord, Yahweh.” Here Adon (“Lord” or “Master”) is used, not Adonai.

This command is repeated in 34:26 and Deuteronomy 14:21. Its original purpose is uncertain; it may forbid a Canaanite ritual or express respect for the bond between mother and young. It became the basis of the Jewish practice of not mixing meat and milk.
Or “panic” or “plague.” The meaning of the Hebrew word tsir‘ah is uncertain.
That is, the Mediterranean Sea.
That is, the Euphrates.

verses.text: Then he said to Moses, “Come up to Yahweh, you and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and worship at a distance.
Moses alone is to come near to Yahweh, but the others are not to come near, and the people are not to come up with him.”
Moses came and told the people all the words of Yahweh and all the rules. All the people answered with one voice and said, “All the words that Yahweh has spoken we will do.”
Moses wrote down all the words of Yahweh. He rose early in the morning and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars, for the twelve tribes of Israel.
He sent young men of the Israelites, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of bulls to Yahweh.
Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he splashed against the altar.
Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. They said, “All that Yahweh has spoken we will do, and we will obey.”
Moses took the blood and splashed it on the people and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that Yahweh has made with you in accordance with all these words.”{a}
Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up.
They saw the God of Israel.{b} Under his feet there was something like a pavement of lapis lazuli,{c} like the very sky for clearness.
But he did not lay his hand on the leaders{d} of the Israelites. They beheld God, and they ate and drank.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain and stay there, and I will give you the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment that I have written for their instruction.”
So Moses set out with Joshua his assistant, and Moses went up the mountain of God.
He said to the elders, “Stay here for us until we come back to you; and see, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever has a legal matter may go to them.”
Then Moses went up the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain.
The glory of Yahweh settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. On the seventh day he called to Moses from the midst of the cloud.
The appearance of the glory of Yahweh was like a consuming fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the Israelites.
Moses entered the cloud and went up the mountain. Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

notes.text: Jesus echoes these words at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:28; Mark 14:24); compare Hebrews 9:18–20.
The Septuagint reads “they saw the place where the God of Israel stood,” and in verse 11 “they appeared in the place of God,” softening the statement that they saw God.
Or “sapphire.” The ancient sapphire was probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.
Hebrew atsilim, “corners” or “nobles,” a rare word.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the Israelites, that they bring me a contribution;{a} from every man whose heart prompts him you shall take my contribution.
This is the offering that you are to receive from them: gold, silver, and bronze;{b}
blue, purple, and scarlet yarn,{c} fine linen, and goats’ hair;
rams’ skins dyed red, fine leather,{d} and acacia wood;{e}
oil for the light, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense;
onyx stones{f} and stones to be set, for the ephod{g} and for the breastpiece.
Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.
Exactly as I show you, the pattern of the tabernacle{h} and the pattern of all its furnishings, so you are to make it.
“They are to make an ark{i} of acacia wood, about 3¾ feet long, 2¼ feet wide, and 2¼ feet high.{j}
You are to overlay it with pure gold, inside and outside you are to overlay it, and you are to make a molding of gold around it.
You are to cast four rings of gold for it and fasten them on its four feet, two rings on one side of it and two rings on the other side.
You are to make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.
You are to put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark, to carry the ark by them.
The poles are to remain in the rings of the ark; they must not be removed from it.
You are to put into the ark the testimony{k} that I will give you.
“You are to make an atonement cover{l} of pure gold, about 3¾ feet long and 2¼ feet wide.{m}
You shall make two cherubim{n} of gold; make them of beaten work, at the two ends of the mercy seat.
Make one cherub at the one end, and at the other end the other; the cherubim you shall make of one piece with the mercy seat, at its two ends.
The cherubim shall spread their wings upward, covering the mercy seat with their wings, and their faces shall look toward each other; toward the mercy seat shall be the faces of the cherubim.
You shall place the mercy seat on the top of the ark, and into the ark you shall put the testimony that I shall give you.
There I will meet with you; from above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim over the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about all that I shall command you for the Israelites.
“You are to make a table of acacia wood, about 3 feet long, 1½ feet wide, and 2¼ feet high.{o}
You are to overlay it with pure gold and make a molding of gold around it.
You are to make a rim around it about 3 inches wide,{p} and make a molding of gold around the rim.
You are to make four rings of gold for it and fasten the rings at the four corners at its four legs.
Close to the rim the rings shall be, as places for the poles to carry the table.
You are to make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold, and the table is to be carried with them.
You are to make its plates and its dishes, its jars and its bowls for pouring out drink offerings; you are to make them of pure gold.
And you are to set the bread of the Presence{q} on the table before me always.
“You shall make a lampstand{r} of pure gold; of hammered work the lampstand shall be made, its base and its stem; its cups, its knobs,{s} and its flowers shall be of one piece with it.
Six branches are to go out from its sides, three branches of the lampstand from one side of it and three branches of the lampstand from the other side of it.

On one branch are to be three cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with a knob and a flower, and on the next branch three cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with a knob and a flower; so for the six branches going out from the lampstand.
On the lampstand itself are to be four cups shaped like almond blossoms, with their knobs and flowers,

and a knob under the first pair of branches, of one piece with it, and a knob under the second pair of branches, of one piece with it, and a knob under the third pair of branches, of one piece with it, for the six branches going out from the lampstand.
Their knobs and their branches shall be of one piece with it; all of it one piece of hammered work of pure gold.
You shall make its seven lamps; and the lamps shall be set up to give light on the area in front of it.
Its snuffers and its trays are to be of pure gold.
It is to be made, with all these utensils, from about 75 pounds of pure gold.{t}
See that you make them after the pattern for them that you were shown on the mountain.

notes.text: Hebrew terumah, a contribution set apart, literally “something lifted off.”
Or “copper.” Hebrew nehoshet means copper or its alloy bronze.
The colors came from dyes: blue (or violet) from sea snails, purple from murex shells, and scarlet from an insect dye.
Hebrew tahash. The meaning is uncertain; suggestions include the skins of dolphins or dugongs (sea cows), goatskin, or leather dyed a particular color.
Acacia is a hard, durable desert wood that grows in Sinai.
Or “carnelian.” The identification of many ancient stones is uncertain.
The ephod was an outer priestly garment, apparently a kind of apron or vest (28:6–14).
Hebrew mishkan, “dwelling place,” from shakan, “to dwell” (verse 8). It was a portable tent-shrine.
Hebrew aron, “chest” or “box,” a different word from Noah’s ark.

Hebrew “two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high,” about 1.1 meters long and 0.7 meter wide and high. A cubit, the distance from elbow to fingertip, was about 18 inches (45 centimeters); a longer cubit of about 20.5 inches (52 centimeters) was also used, so the measurements in these chapters may be somewhat larger.
That is, the two tablets of stone, which bore witness to the covenant (31:18).

Hebrew kapporet, from the verb kipper, “to atone” or “to cover.” The traditional English “mercy seat” comes from Luther’s Gnadenstuhl and Tyndale. The Septuagint reads hilasterion, “place of atonement” (compare Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:5).
Hebrew “two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide,” about 1.1 by 0.7 meters.
Cherubim (singular cherub) were winged heavenly beings, often pictured in the ancient Near East as guardians of thrones and holy places. Compare Genesis 3:24.
Hebrew “two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high,” about 90 centimeters long, 45 wide, and 70 high.
Hebrew “a handbreadth,” about 3 inches (7.5 centimeters).
Literally “bread of the face,” twelve loaves set before Yahweh and renewed every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9).
Hebrew menorah.
Hebrew kaftor, probably the bulb or calyx beneath the flower.
Hebrew “a talent of pure gold,” about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).

verses.text: “You are to make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twisted linen, and blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; you are to make them with cherubim worked into them by a skilled designer.
The length of each curtain is to be about 42 feet, and the width of each curtain about 6 feet;{a} all the curtains are to have the same measurements.
Five curtains are to be joined to one another, and the other five curtains are to be joined to one another.
You are to make loops of blue on the edge of the outermost curtain in the first set, and likewise make them on the edge of the outermost curtain in the second set.
You shall make fifty loops in the one curtain, and fifty loops in the edge of the curtain that is in the second set, so that the loops are opposite one another.
You shall make fifty clasps of gold, and couple the curtains to one another with the clasps, so that the tabernacle may be one.
“You shall also make curtains of goats’ hair for a tent over the tabernacle; eleven curtains you shall make.
The length of each curtain is to be about 45 feet, and the width of each curtain about 6 feet;{b} the eleven curtains are to have the same measurements.
You are to join five curtains by themselves and six curtains by themselves, and you are to fold the sixth curtain double at the front of the tent.
You are to make fifty loops on the edge of the outermost curtain in the first set and fifty loops on the edge of the curtain in the second set.
And you shall make fifty hooks of bronze, and put the hooks into the loops, and join the tent together, that it may be one.
And the overlapping part that remains of the curtains of the tent, the half curtain that remains, shall hang over the back of the tabernacle.
The extra length of the curtains of the tent, about 18 inches{c} on one side and about 18 inches on the other, is to hang over the sides of the tabernacle, on this side and that, to cover it.
You are to make for the tent a covering of rams’ skins dyed red, and a covering of fine leather above that.
“You are to make upright frames{d} of acacia wood for the tabernacle.
The length of each frame is to be about 15 feet, and the width of each frame about 2¼ feet.{e}
Each frame is to have two tenons,{f} joined to one another. You are to make all the frames of the tabernacle this way.
You shall make the frames for the tabernacle: twenty frames on the south side, toward the south;
Forty sockets{g} of silver you shall make under the twenty boards: two sockets under the one board for its two tenons, and two sockets under the next board for its two tenons;
and for the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, twenty frames,
and their forty sockets of silver, two sockets under the one board, and two sockets under the next board.
And for the rear of the tabernacle toward the west you shall make six frames.
You are to make two frames for the corners of the tabernacle at the rear.
They are to be doubled at the bottom and likewise complete{h} at the top, up to the first ring. So it is to be for both of them; they will form the two corners.
There shall be eight boards, and their sockets of silver, sixteen sockets; two sockets under the one board, and two sockets under the next board.
“You shall make bars of acacia wood; five for the boards of one side of the tabernacle,
and five bars for the boards of the other side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the boards of the side of the tabernacle at the rear toward the west.
The middle crossbar, halfway up the frames, is to run from end to end.
You shall overlay the boards with gold, and make their rings of gold for places for the bars, and you shall overlay the bars with gold.
And you shall raise up the tabernacle according to the plan that was shown you on the mountain.
“You shall make a veil{i} of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen; with cherubim skillfully worked into it it shall be made.
You are to hang it on four posts of acacia overlaid with gold, with hooks of gold, set on four bases of silver.
And you shall hang the veil under the hooks, and bring the ark of the testimony in behind the veil; the veil shall make a division for you between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place.{j}
You shall set the mercy seat upon the ark of the testimony in the Most Holy Place.
And you shall set the table outside the veil, with the lampstand opposite the table on the south side of the tabernacle; the table you shall put on the north side.
“You shall make a hanging for the door of the tent, embroidered with needlework, of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine twisted linen.
And you shall make for the hanging five pillars of acacia wood and overlay them with gold; their hooks shall be of gold, and you shall cast five sockets of bronze for them.

notes.text: Hebrew “twenty-eight cubits” long and “four cubits” wide, about 12.6 by 1.8 meters. On the cubit, see the note at 25:10.
Hebrew “thirty cubits” long and “four cubits” wide, about 13.5 by 1.8 meters.
Hebrew “a cubit,” about 45 centimeters.
Hebrew qerashim, traditionally “boards.” They may have been open frameworks rather than solid planks.
Hebrew “ten cubits” long and “a cubit and a half” wide, about 4.5 by 0.7 meters.
Hebrew “hands,” projections fitting into the bases.
Or “sockets,” hollow bases into which the tenons fit.
Or “joined.” The construction of the corner frames is uncertain.
Hebrew parokhet, the inner curtain that closed off the Most Holy Place.
Hebrew “the holy of holies.”

verses.text: “You are to make the altar of acacia wood, about 7½ feet long and 7½ feet wide. The altar is to be square, and it is to be about 4½ feet high.{a}
You are to make its horns{b} on its four corners; its horns are to be of one piece with it, and you are to overlay it with bronze.
You are to make its pots for removing its ashes, and its shovels, its basins, its forks, and its firepans. You are to make all its utensils of bronze.
You shall make for it a grating of bronze network, and upon the network you shall make four bronze rings at its four corners.
You are to set it under the ledge of the altar, so that the network extends halfway down the altar.
You are to make poles for the altar, poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with bronze.
Its poles shall be put into the rings, and the poles shall be on the two sides of the altar, to carry it.
You are to make it hollow, of boards. As it was shown you on the mountain, so are they to make it.
“You shall make the court of the tabernacle. On the south side, toward the south, the court shall have hangings of fine twisted linen, about 150 feet in length{c} for one side;
with their twenty posts and their twenty bases of bronze; the hooks of the posts and their bands{d} are to be of silver.
Likewise for the north side, the length is to be hangings about 150 feet long, with their twenty posts and their twenty bases of bronze; the hooks of the posts and their bands are to be of silver.
And for the breadth of the court on the west side there shall be hangings of about 75 feet,{e} with ten pillars and ten sockets.
The width of the courtyard on the front, to the east, is to be about 75 feet.
The hangings for one side of the entrance are to be about 22½ feet long,{f} with their three posts and their three bases.
On the other side the hangings are to be about 22½ feet long, with their three posts and their three bases.
And for the gate of the court a hanging of about 30 feet{g} of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen, embroidered with needlework; their pillars four, and their sockets four.
All the posts around the courtyard are to be banded with silver; their hooks are to be of silver and their bases of bronze.
The length of the courtyard is to be about 150 feet, the width about 75 feet throughout,{h} and the height about 7½ feet,{i} with hangings of fine twisted linen and bases of bronze.
All the utensils of the tabernacle for all its service, and all its tent pegs and all the tent pegs of the courtyard, are to be of bronze.
“And you shall command the Israelites to bring you pure olive oil, beaten, for the light, to make a lamp burn continually.

In the tent of meeting,{j} outside the curtain that hangs before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall keep the lamp in order, from dusk until dawn, before Yahweh. It shall be an everlasting statute for the Israelites, throughout their generations.

notes.text: Hebrew “five cubits long and five cubits wide … three cubits high,” about 2.3 meters square and 1.4 meters high.
Projections shaped like horns at the corners of the altar, the holiest part of it (29:12).
Hebrew “a hundred cubits,” about 45 meters. So also in verses 11 and 18.
Or “connecting rods.”
Hebrew “fifty cubits,” about 23 meters. So also in verses 13 and 18.
Hebrew “fifteen cubits,” about 6.8 meters. So also in verse 15.
Hebrew “twenty cubits,” about 9 meters.
Hebrew “fifty by fifty,” which may mean fifty cubits at each end.
Hebrew “five cubits,” about 2.3 meters.
Hebrew ohel mo’ed, the tent where Yahweh met with Moses and the people (29:42–43). It is another name for the tabernacle.

verses.text: “And bring near to you Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, from among the Israelites, that he may minister to me as priest—Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s sons.
You are to make holy garments for your brother Aaron, for glory and for beauty.
And you shall speak to all who are wise of heart,{a} whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they make Aaron’s garments to sanctify him, that he may minister to me as priest.

These are the garments that they shall make: a breastplate and an ephod, a robe and a woven tunic, a turban and a sash. They shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother and for his sons, that he may minister to me as priest.
They are to use gold, blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen.
“They shall make the ephod of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine twisted linen, artistically worked.
It shall have two shoulder straps joined to its two edges, so that it is joined together.
The skillfully woven band{b} on it, which is on it, is to be of the same workmanship and of one piece with it, of gold, of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and of fine twisted linen.
You are to take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel,
six of their names on one stone, and the names of the remaining six on the other stone, in the order of their birth.
As a jeweler engraves a seal, you are to engrave the two stones with the names of the sons of Israel. You are to set them in settings of gold filigree.
You are to put the two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel. Aaron is to bear their names before Yahweh on his two shoulders for remembrance.
You are to make settings of gold filigree,
and two chains of pure gold, twisted like cords, and fasten the corded chains to the settings.
“You shall make the breastplate of judgment, artistically worked; like the work of the ephod you shall make it, with gold and with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with fine twisted linen.
It is to be square and folded double, about 9 inches long and about 9 inches wide.{c}
You are to set in it settings of stones, four rows of stones. A row of carnelian, topaz, and emerald{d} is to be the first row;
the second row a turquoise, a lapis lazuli, and a diamond;{e}
the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst;
and the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. They are to be set in gold filigree.
And the stones shall be twelve, corresponding to the names of the sons of Israel; they shall be engraved like a signet with each one’s name, for the twelve tribes.
You are to make for the breastpiece twisted chains like cords, of pure gold.
You are to make for the breastpiece two rings of gold and put the two rings on the two ends of the breastpiece.
You are to put the two cords of gold in the two rings at the ends of the breastpiece.
The other two ends of the two cords you are to attach to the two settings, and so attach them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front.
You shall make two rings of gold, and put them on the two ends of the breastplate, on its edge, which is toward the ephod on the inside.
You are to make two rings of gold and attach them to the lower part of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, on its front, near its seam, above the skillfully woven band of the ephod.

They shall tie the breastplate by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a blue cord, so that it is above the skillfully woven band of the ephod, and the breastplate does not come loose from the ephod.
So Aaron shall carry the names of the sons of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, for a memorial continually before Yahweh.

In the breastpiece of judgment you are to put the Urim and the Thummim,{f} and they are to be over Aaron’s heart when he goes in before Yahweh. So Aaron is to bear the judgment of the Israelites over his heart before Yahweh continually.
“You are to make the robe of the ephod all of blue.
In the middle of it there shall be an opening for the head, and around its opening there shall be a woven binding, like the opening of a coat of mail,{g} so that it will not tear.
On its hem you are to make pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, around its hem, with bells of gold between them all around:
a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, around the hem of the robe.
It is to be on Aaron when he ministers, and its sound is to be heard when he goes into the Holy Place before Yahweh and when he comes out, so that he will not die.
“You are to make a plate{h} of pure gold and engrave on it, like the engraving of a seal, ‘Holy to Yahweh.’
You are to fasten it on the turban by a cord of blue; it is to be on the front of the turban.

It shall be upon the forehead of Aaron, that he may bear the iniquity connected with the holy things which the Israelites hallow with all their holy gifts; and it shall be on his forehead continually, that they may find acceptance before Yahweh.
“You shall weave the tunic in checker work of fine linen, and you shall make a turban of fine linen, and a sash of needlework.
For Aaron’s sons you are to make tunics, sashes, and headbands; you are to make them for glory and for beauty.
So you shall put them on Aaron your brother and on his sons with him; and you shall anoint them, consecrate them,{i} and sanctify them, that they may minister to me as priests.
You are to make linen undergarments for them to cover their naked flesh. They are to reach from the waist to the thighs.

They shall be on Aaron and on his sons whenever they enter the tent of meeting, or approach the altar to minister in the Holy Place, so that they do not bear iniquity and die. It shall be a statute forever for him and for his descendants after him.

notes.text: Hebrew “wise of heart.” The Hebrew word hokhmah, “wisdom,” here means practical skill.
Or “waistband,” a belt woven as part of the ephod.
Hebrew “a span long and a span wide,” about 23 centimeters square. A span, the distance from thumb to little finger with the hand spread, was half a cubit, about 9 inches.
The identification of several of these stones is uncertain; the English names follow the Septuagint and modern proposals. Compare the stones of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:19–20.
Hebrew yahalom, perhaps a hard stone such as jasper or onyx. Diamonds were probably not cut in ancient Israel.

The Urim and Thummim were objects kept in the breastpiece and used to learn God’s will (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 28:6). Their form and use are uncertain. The words may mean “lights and perfections,” or they may begin with the first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet.
The meaning of the Hebrew word tahra is uncertain; it may mean a leather collar or the neck opening of a garment.
Hebrew tsits, “flower” or “shining thing,” perhaps a rosette-shaped plate.
Hebrew “fill their hand,” an expression for installing priests in office.

verses.text: “Now this is the thing you shall do to them to consecrate them, that they may minister to me as priests: take one young bull and two rams without blemish,
and unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil. You are to make them of fine wheat flour.
And you shall put them into one basket, and bring them in the basket, with the bull and the two rams.
You are to bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water.
You are to take the garments and put on Aaron the tunic, the robe of the ephod, the ephod, and the breastpiece, and tie the skillfully woven band of the ephod around him.
You are to set the turban on his head and put the holy crown{a} on the turban.
You are to take the anointing oil, pour it on his head, and anoint him.
Then you are to bring his sons and put tunics on them.
You are to tie sashes on them, Aaron and his sons, and bind headbands on them. The priesthood is to be theirs by a statute forever. So you are to ordain Aaron and his sons.
“You are to bring the bull before the tent of meeting. Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on the head of the bull.
Then you are to slaughter the bull before Yahweh at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
You are to take some of the blood of the bull and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger, and you are to pour out all the rest of the blood at the base of the altar.
You are to take all the fat that covers the entrails, the lobe of the liver,{b} the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and burn them on the altar.
But the flesh of the bull, together with its skin and its dung, you shall burn up with fire outside the camp. It is a sin offering.{c}
“Then you are to take one of the rams, and Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on the head of the ram.
You are to slaughter the ram, take its blood, and splash it against the altar on all sides.
You are to cut the ram into its pieces, wash its entrails and its legs, and put them with its pieces and its head.
You are to burn the whole ram on the altar. It is a burnt offering to Yahweh, a pleasing aroma, an offering by fire to Yahweh.
“You are to take the other ram, and Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on the head of the ram.

Then you shall kill the ram, and take some of its blood and put it on the tip of the right ear of Aaron and on the tips of the right ears of his sons, and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the big toes of their right feet, and sprinkle the blood all around on the altar.

And you shall take some of the blood that is on the altar, and some of the anointing oil, and sprinkle it on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and their garments with him; so he will be consecrated, and his garments, and his sons and their garments with him.

“You are to take the fat from the ram, the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails, the lobe of the liver, the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and the right thigh, for it is a ram of ordination;
and one loaf of bread, one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer, out of the basket of unleavened bread that is before Yahweh.
And you shall put all these in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons, and wave them as a wave offering{d} before Yahweh.
Then you are to take them from their hands and burn them on the altar on top of the burnt offering, as a pleasing aroma before Yahweh. It is an offering by fire to Yahweh.
“Then you shall take the breast from the ram of Aaron’s consecration and wave it as a wave offering before Yahweh; and it shall be your portion.

You are to consecrate the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution, which is waved and which is lifted up, from the ram of ordination, from what is Aaron’s and from what is his sons’.

It shall be Aaron’s and his sons’ as a perpetual portion from the Israelites, for it is a contribution; it shall be an offering from the Israelites out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings,{e} their offering to Yahweh.
“The holy garments of Aaron are to belong to his sons after him, so that they may be anointed in them and ordained in them.
The son who becomes priest in his place, who comes into the tent of meeting to minister in the Holy Place, is to wear them seven days.
“You are to take the ram of ordination and boil its flesh in a holy place.
Aaron and his sons are to eat the flesh of the ram and the bread that is in the basket at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
They are to eat those things by which atonement was made, to ordain and consecrate them, but no outsider{f} may eat them, because they are holy.
If any of the flesh of the ordination or of the bread remains until the morning, you are to burn what remains with fire. It must not be eaten, because it is holy.
“So you are to do for Aaron and for his sons, according to all that I have commanded you. Through seven days you are to ordain them.
And each day you shall offer a bull as a sin offering for atonement, and you shall cleanse the altar when you make atonement for it, and you shall anoint it to hallow it.
For seven days you are to make atonement for the altar and consecrate it. Then the altar will be most holy; whatever touches the altar will become holy.
“This is what you are to offer on the altar: two lambs a year old, day by day, continually.
One lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight.{g}
With the first lamb there is to be about 2 quarts of fine flour{h} mixed with about 1 quart of beaten oil,{i} and about 1 quart of wine for a drink offering.
The other lamb you are to offer at twilight, and offer with it a grain offering and its drink offering as in the morning, for a pleasing aroma, an offering by fire to Yahweh.
It is to be a continual burnt offering throughout your generations at the entrance of the tent of meeting before Yahweh, where I will meet with you, to speak to you there.
There I will meet with the Israelites, and it will be made holy by my glory.
So I will hallow the tent of meeting and the altar. I will also hallow both Aaron and his sons to minister to me as priests.
I will dwell among the Israelites and will be their God.
They will know that I am Yahweh their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them. I am Yahweh their God.

notes.text: That is, the gold plate inscribed “Holy to Yahweh” (28:36).
Or “the appendage of the liver.” The exact organ is uncertain.
Hebrew hatta’t, also translated “purification offering.”
Hebrew tenufah, an offering presented by moving it toward the altar and back, or lifting it up.
Hebrew shelamim, also translated “fellowship offerings” or “offerings of well-being.”
Hebrew zar, a person not of the priestly family.
Hebrew “between the two evenings,” understood either as between sunset and dark or as between midafternoon and sunset. So also in verse 41.
Hebrew “a tenth,” meaning a tenth of an ephah, about 2.2 liters.
Hebrew “a quarter of a hin,” about 0.9 liter. A hin was about 1 gallon (3.7 liters); estimates of ancient liquid measures vary.

verses.text: “You shall make an altar to burn incense on; of acacia wood you shall make it.
It shall be about 18 inches long and 18 inches wide—square—and about 3 feet high;{a} its horns shall be of one piece with it.
You shall overlay it with pure gold—its top, its sides all around, and its horns—and make a gold molding around it.
Two gold rings you shall make for it, under its molding, on its two sides; you shall make them on opposite sides, and they shall be holders for the poles with which to carry it.
You are to make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.
And you shall put it before the veil that is by the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat that is over the testimony, where I will meet with you.
Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it. Every morning when he tends the lamps he is to burn it,
and when Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight{b} he is to burn it, a perpetual incense before Yahweh throughout your generations.
You must not offer unauthorized incense on it, or a burnt offering, or a grain offering, and you must not pour a drink offering on it.

Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once in the year; with the blood of the sin offering of atonement he shall make atonement upon it, once in the year throughout your generations. It is most holy to Yahweh.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“When you take a census of the Israelites to count them, each man is to give a ransom for his life to Yahweh when you count them, so that there may be no plague among them when you count them.
Everyone who is counted is to give this: a fifth of an ounce of silver,{c} by the sanctuary standard. This is the offering to Yahweh.
Everyone who is counted, from twenty years old and upward, is to give the offering to Yahweh.
The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than a fifth of an ounce, when they give the offering of Yahweh to make atonement for your lives.

And you shall take the atonement money of the Israelites and appoint it for the service of the tent of meeting, that it may be a memorial for the Israelites before Yahweh, to make atonement for your lives.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“You shall also make a basin of bronze, with a stand of bronze, for washing. Set it between the tent of meeting and the altar, and put water in it.
Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and their feet in it.
When they go into the tent of meeting, they shall wash with water, lest they die; or when they come near the altar to minister, by presenting an offering made by fire to Yahweh,
they are to wash their hands and their feet, so that they will not die. It is to be a statute forever for them, for him and his descendants throughout their generations.”
Moreover, Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Take for yourself the finest spices: of liquid myrrh about 12½ pounds,{d} of fragrant cinnamon half as much, about 6¼ pounds,{e} of fragrant cane{f} about 6¼ pounds,
of cassia about 12½ pounds, by the sanctuary standard,{g} and about a gallon of olive oil.{h}
You are to make from these a holy anointing oil, a fragrant blend, the work of a perfumer. It is to be a holy anointing oil.
With it you are to anoint the tent of meeting, the ark of the testimony,
the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense,
the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin and its stand.
You are to consecrate them, so that they may be most holy. Whatever touches them will become holy.
You are to anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, so that they may serve me as priests.
You are to speak to the Israelites, saying, ‘This is to be a holy anointing oil to me throughout your generations.
It must not be poured on anyone’s body,{i} and you must not make any like it with the same formula. It is holy, and it is to be holy to you.
Whoever blends any like it, or whoever puts any of it on an outsider, is to be cut off from his people.’”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Take for yourself sweet spices, stacte,{j} onycha, and galbanum, sweet spices with pure frankincense, of each an equal part.
You are to make from it incense, a blend, the work of a perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy.
You shall grind part of it into fine powder and set some before the testimony in the tent of meeting, where I will meet with you. It shall be most holy to you.
The incense that you make according to its formula, you must not make for yourselves. It is to be holy to you for Yahweh.
Whoever makes any like it, to enjoy its fragrance, is to be cut off from his people.”

notes.text: Hebrew “a cubit long and a cubit wide … two cubits high,” about 45 centimeters square and 90 centimeters high.
Hebrew “between the two evenings.” See the note at 12:6.

Hebrew “half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs),” about 5.7 grams. A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams) and a gerah one-twentieth of a shekel. The “sanctuary shekel” may have been a standard kept at the sanctuary, or a heavier shekel; weights varied over time. In verse 15, Hebrew “half a shekel.”
Hebrew “five hundred shekels,” about 5.75 kilograms. So also for the cassia in verse 24.
Hebrew “two hundred fifty shekels,” about 2.9 kilograms. So also for the cane.
Or “calamus,” an aromatic reed. The identification of several of these spices is uncertain.
Hebrew “by the shekel of the sanctuary.” See the note at verse 13.
Hebrew “a hin of olive oil,” about 3.7 liters.
Hebrew “on the flesh of man,” that is, on ordinary people.
The identity of stacte (Hebrew nataf, “drops”), onycha (Hebrew shehelet, perhaps from a shellfish), and galbanum (a plant resin) is not certain.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“See, I have called by name Bezalel{a} son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, in knowledge, and in every kind of workmanship,
to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, in silver, and in bronze,
in cutting jewels for setting, in carving wood, and in every kind of workmanship.

And I, look, I have appointed with him Oholiab{b} son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And in the hearts of all who are skilled I have put skill, so that they may make all that I have commanded you:
the tent of meeting, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is upon it, and all the furniture of the tent—
the table and its utensils, the pure lampstand with all its utensils, the altar of incense,
the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, the basin and its stand,
the finely woven{c} garments, the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests,
the anointing oil, and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. They are to do according to all that I have commanded you.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,

“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘Above all you are to keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, so that you may know that I am Yahweh who makes you holy.{d}
You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy to you. Everyone who profanes it shall surely be put to death; anyone who does work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people.
Six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest,{e} holy to Yahweh. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day must be put to death.
So the Israelites are to keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations as a perpetual covenant.
It is a sign between me and the Israelites forever, for in six days Yahweh made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.’”
When he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, he gave to Moses the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God.

notes.text: Bezalel means “in the shadow (protection) of God.”
Oholiab means “the father is my tent.”
Or “the woven,” or “the service.” The meaning of the Hebrew word serad is uncertain.
Hebrew YHWH meqaddishkem, “Yahweh who sanctifies you.” Compare Leviticus 20:8.
Hebrew shabbat shabbaton, “a Sabbath of Sabbath rest.”

verses.text: When the people saw that Moses was slow to come down from the mountain, the people assembled before Aaron and said to him, “Rise up, make us gods{a} that shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.”
Aaron said to them, “Take off the gold rings that are in the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me.”
So all the people tore off the gold rings that were in their ears and brought them to Aaron.

He received the gold from their hand, fashioned it with an engraving tool,{b} and made it into a cast-metal calf. And they said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!”
When Aaron saw it, he built an altar before it; and Aaron made a proclamation and said, “Tomorrow is a feast to Yahweh.”
They rose early on the next day, and offered burnt offerings and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.{c}
Yahweh said to Moses, “Go, get down, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have acted corruptly.

They have quickly turned aside from the way I commanded them. They have made for themselves a calf of molten metal, and have bowed down to it and sacrificed to it, saying, ‘These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!’”
Yahweh said to Moses, “I have seen this people, and look, it is a stiff-necked people.
Now therefore leave me alone, so that my anger may burn against them and I may consume them; and I will make of you a great nation.”
But Moses implored Yahweh his God and said, “Yahweh, why does your anger burn against your people, whom you have brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand?

Why should the Egyptians say, ‘With harmful intent did he bring them out, to slay them among the mountains and to blot them from the surface of the earth’? Turn from your fierce anger, and relent{d} concerning this evil against your people.

Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self and declared, ‘I will make your descendants multiply like the stars of heaven, and all this land that I have spoken of I will give to your descendants, and they shall inherit it forever.’”
And Yahweh relented from the harm that he had said he would do to his people.
Moses turned and went down from the mountain, the two tablets of the testimony in his hand, tablets written on both their sides; on the one side and on the other they were written.
The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.
When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, “There is a sound of war in the camp.”
But he said, “It is not the voice of those who shout for victory, nor the voice of those who cry in defeat; the voice of singing{e} I hear.”
As soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses’ anger blazed hot, and he cast the tablets from his hands and shattered them at the base of the mountain.
He took the calf that they had made, burned it with fire, ground it to powder, scattered it on the water, and made the Israelites drink it.
Moses said to Aaron, “What did this people do to you, that you have brought so great a sin on them?”
Aaron said, “Do not let the anger of my lord burn. You know the people, that they are set on evil.
For they said to me, ‘Make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’
So I said to them, ‘Whoever has any gold, take it off.’ So they gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf.”
Moses saw that the people were out of control—for Aaron had let them get out of control, to be a laughingstock among their adversaries—
then Moses stood in the entrance of the camp and said, “Who is on Yahweh’s side? Let him come to me.” And all the sons of Levi gathered themselves to him.

He said to them, “This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let every man put his sword on his thigh and go to and fro, from gate to gate throughout the camp, and let every man slay his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.’”
The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses. About three thousand men of the people fell that day.
Moses said, “Ordain yourselves{f} today for Yahweh, each one at the cost of his son and his brother, so that he may give you a blessing this day.”
The next day Moses said to the people, “You have sinned a great sin. And now I will go up to Yahweh; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin.”
So Moses returned to Yahweh and said, “Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. They have made themselves gods of gold.
But now, if you will forgive their sin… But if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written.”
But Yahweh said to Moses, “Whoever has sinned against me, him I will blot out of my book.
But now go, lead the people to the place of which I spoke to you. See, my angel shall go before you; nevertheless, in the day when I visit, I will bring their sin upon them.”
Then Yahweh struck the people with a plague, because they made the calf, the one that Aaron made.

notes.text: Or “a god.” Hebrew elohim with a plural verb; the same form is used in verses 4, 8, and 23. Compare 1 Kings 12:28.
Or “bound it in a bag.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew verb tsahaq can include revelry or sexual play. Compare 1 Corinthians 10:7.
Or “change your mind.” Hebrew niham, used also in verse 14.
Hebrew “of answering,” perhaps singing in response, or antiphonal singing. The Septuagint reads “of those who begin a song over wine.”
Hebrew “Fill your hands,” the expression for ordination to priestly service (28:41). The Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, and Vulgate read, “You have ordained yourselves.”

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Go, set out from here, you and the people whom you brought up from the land of Egypt, to the land of which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, saying, ‘To your offspring I will give it.’
I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey. But I will not go up among you, for you are a stiff-necked people, or I might consume you on the way.”
When the people heard this harsh word, they mourned, and no one put on his ornaments.

For Yahweh had said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites, ‘You are a stubborn people. If I should go up among you even for a moment, I would consume you. So now take your ornaments off, and I will decide what to do with you.’”
So the Israelites stripped themselves of their ornaments from Mount Horeb onward.

Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, at a distance from the camp, and he called it the tent of meeting.{a} And everyone who sought Yahweh went out to the tent of meeting that was outside the camp.
Whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would rise and stand, each at the entrance of his own tent, and watch Moses until he had gone into the tent.
Whenever Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would come down and stand at the entrance of the tent, and Yahweh{b} would speak with Moses.
